lessons.title: Start here · Your AI Testing 2.0 preparation route
lessons.summary: Understand the CT-AI exam, its weighted K3 questions and how to keep mock papers fresh.

blocks.text: This independent English study pack is aligned to the ISTQB Certified Tester AI Testing (CT-AI) syllabus v2.0, released on 2026-04-17. It is not an official exam or an accredited training course. CT-AI v2.0 replaces v1.0: the new syllabus concentrates on testing AI-based systems, especially machine learning systems, and leaves the use of AI as a testing tool to the separate CT-GenAI certification. The ISTQB Foundation Level (CTFL) certificate is the entry requirement for the CT-AI exam, so these lessons assume Foundation vocabulary such as test level, test oracle, risk-based testing and confirmation testing.

blocks.title: Exam format
blocks.text: The full simulation has 40 questions, 60 minutes and 44 available points. 36 questions are K2 (one point each) and four are K3 application questions worth two points each, one from each of AI-3.3.1 (metric calculation), AI-4.2.2 (red teaming), AI-5.1.5 (dataset constraint testing) and AI-6.1.5 (metamorphic testing). The pass mark is 29 points (65%). Select-TWO questions require exactly two answers and award nothing for a partial answer. The 75-minute version models the 25% extension for candidates taking the exam in a non-native language; your exam provider decides eligibility.

blocks.title: A practical route
blocks.text: First pass: read the lessons in order, including every 'Syllabus details to know' block, and solve each self-check before reading its solution. Second pass: practise the four K3 skills until they are routine: confusion-matrix metrics, a red-teaming plan, dataset constraints and metamorphic relations. Third pass: take paper A under timed conditions, review every wrong answer and every guess, revisit the linked lesson, then take papers B to D on separate days.

blocks.title: Fresh evidence
blocks.text: The four papers contain different questions and share no question families. The 75-minute version of a paper repeats its questions. Learning sessions and 20-question short practice draw from the whole bank, including paper questions, so they can use up a paper's freshness. LearnForge's readiness rule needs strictly more than 90% on each of three full mocks with fresh families, so keep at least three papers unopened until you are ready to measure. A simulated pass (29 of 44 points) is reported separately from that recommendation.

blocks.title: How the chapters fit together
blocks.text: Chapter 1 introduces AI, generative AI, hardware, hosting, frameworks and regulation. Chapter 2 adds the AI-specific quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25059 and shows acceptance criteria for them. Chapter 3 explains how machine learning models are built: forms of learning, the ML workflow, data preparation, datasets, metrics and neural networks. Chapter 4 explains why AI-based systems are harder to test (locked versus adaptive behavior, statistics, test oracles), how to test generative AI and red-team it, and which test levels and risks apply. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 are the practical core: input data testing, model testing and ML development testing, each starting from a risk-to-mitigation table.

blocks.title: Read beyond the objective list
blocks.text: All syllabus sections are examinable except the introduction, hands-on objectives, references and appendices (CT-AI v2.0, section 0.6, p. 10). Keywords listed under each chapter heading must be remembered with their glossary definitions. Questions may combine material from more than one section. Hands-on objectives (HO-x) are not examined, but practising them makes the K3 objectives much easier; each lesson includes a hands-on guide you can follow with a spreadsheet or notebook.

blocks.title: Sources and authorship
blocks.text: ISTQB and the authors named in the syllabus own the official syllabus, sample exam and exam-rule documents. This pack contains original explanations, examples and questions; it does not reproduce the official sample exam. K2 means understand (classify, compare, explain, give examples, summarize). K3 means apply a procedure to a given situation (calculate, implement, use). Lesson references and answer explanations give printed page numbers of the v2.0 syllabus.

lessons.title: 1.1 (part 1) · AI systems, AI types and generative AI
lessons.summary: Contrast AI-based and conventional systems, place narrow, general and super AI, and explain AI technologies and generative AI.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A conventional system is programmed imperatively: developers write explicit step-by-step instructions (conditions, loops), so behavior is deterministic and comparatively transparent. Most AI-based systems, especially those using machine learning (ML), are not given explicit rules; they learn patterns from data and apply those patterns to new inputs. Four contrasts matter for testing. Problem solving: AI often relies on probabilistic reasoning, statistical inference and pattern recognition, so outputs are not always predictable. Explainability: deep models may have billions of parameters, so it is hard to say why a decision was made; this matters in healthcare, finance, defence and transport, and is a focus of regulation. Adaptability: conventional systems change only through manual updates, while self-learning AI-based systems can keep changing with new data, which demands continuous monitoring against the core requirements. Predictability: the same input may not give the same output.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A parcel-sorting service routes parcels by postcode using a lookup table written by developers: the same postcode always gives the same chute, and a reviewer can read the rule. A second service reads handwritten addresses with an image model trained on labelled examples: it was never given rules for each handwriting style, its confidence varies, and a reviewer cannot point to the line of code that chose a chute. The second is AI-based; testing it needs statistical evidence and explainability support, not only rule-by-rule checks.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Narrow AI is not 'primitive AI': it covers every AI-based system deployed today, including frontier generative models. General AI (strong AI) does not exist yet. Super AI is not simply 'very large AI'; it improves itself without human control and would surpass human intelligence; the transition is called the technological singularity. Internet access is not a defining condition of super AI.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Classify: (1) a translation model that cannot recognise faces without retraining; (2) a hypothetical system that learns any intellectual task a human can, without retraining per task; (3) a hypothetical system that keeps improving itself beyond human intelligence. Solution: (1) narrow AI; (2) general AI; (3) super AI. A frontier LLM is still narrow AI because it remains task-bounded and has not reached the versatility of general AI.

blocks.title: AI technologies and generative AI
blocks.text:
ML lets systems learn from data without explicit programming. Supervised learning uses labelled data (for example, linear regression and decision trees for prediction and classification). Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data, for example clustering. Reinforcement learning lets an agent learn by trial and error from rewards and penalties. Key ML technologies include neural networks, Bayesian models, support vector machines (SVM) and random forests. Deep learning (DL) is a subset of ML that uses deep neural networks: convolutional networks (CNN) for images and object detection, recurrent networks (RNN) for sequences such as text or time series, and transformers for long-range dependencies in language and, as vision transformers, in images. Other AI technologies include natural language processing, computer vision, fuzzy logic, search algorithms for optimisation and strategy, and rule-based expert systems. Agentic AI adds autonomous agents that plan, reason and act toward goals.

Generative AI (GenAI) creates new content (text, images, video, music, complex data) that resembles its training data; many GenAI systems also classify and predict. The main technologies are generative adversarial networks (two networks in competition produce realistic synthetic data), diffusion models (gradually add and then remove noise) and transformers (self-attention, the basis of LLMs, increasingly multimodal). Most practical GenAI tools are foundation models fine-tuned for specific applications. Concerns include misuse (deepfakes, misinformation, fraud), privacy and manipulation risk, employment impact on white-collar work, and sustainability because training and inference consume a lot of energy. Regulation such as the EU AI Act is emerging to guide responsible use.

blocks.title: Worked case: choosing the right label
blocks.text: A retailer combines three components: a model that groups customers by purchasing behavior without labels; a transformer that drafts product descriptions; and an agent that plans restocking, places orders through tools and adjusts its plan. The first is unsupervised learning (clustering). The second is generative AI built on a transformer, probably a fine-tuned foundation model. The third is agentic AI. Testing each needs a different focus: cluster plausibility, generated-content quality and policy compliance, and safe autonomous actions.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: For each technology, name a typical use: CNN, RNN, transformer, diffusion model, GAN, fuzzy logic, search algorithm, expert system. Then explain in two sentences why a model trained to recognise cat breeds is narrow AI even if it is extremely accurate.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: CNN: image recognition and object detection. RNN: sequential data such as text or sensor time series. Transformer: language processing with long-range context (LLMs) and vision transformers. Diffusion model: high-quality image generation by denoising. GAN: realistic synthetic data from a generator and a discriminator in competition. Fuzzy logic: reasoning under uncertainty. Search algorithm: optimisation such as route finding or strategic decisions. Expert system: structured decision support from explicit rules. The cat-breed model operates within one limited domain and cannot generalise to unrelated tasks without retraining, which is the defining property of narrow AI; accuracy does not change that classification.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Conventional systems: imperative, explicit instructions, deterministic, predictable and transparent. AI-based (ML) systems: learn patterns from data, probabilistic reasoning, statistical inference, outputs not always predictable, explainability challenge (black box), may be self-learning and so need continuous monitoring.
Narrow (weak) AI: specific tasks, all AI deployed today; frontier AI is the most advanced subset of narrow AI (large, highly autonomous GenAI models, still task-specific). General (strong) AI: most intellectual tasks a human can do, without retraining per task; none exists today. Super AI (artificial superintelligence): continuously improves itself without human control, surpasses humans; possible existential risk; transition point = technological singularity.
ML approaches: supervised (labelled data; classification and prediction), unsupervised (clustering), reinforcement (agent, rewards and penalties). ML technologies: neural networks, Bayesian models, SVM, random forests. DL: CNN, RNN, transformers. Other: NLP, computer vision, fuzzy logic, search algorithms, rule-based reasoning/expert systems. Agentic AI: autonomous agents that plan, reason and act.
GenAI: creates new content; technologies GAN, diffusion models, transformers (self-attention); concerns: misuse (deepfakes, misinformation, fraud), privacy/security/manipulation, employment, sustainability (energy, carbon); foundation models fine-tuned for applications; multimodal models; regulation (EU AI Act).

lessons.title: 1.1 (part 2) · Hardware, hosting, frameworks and regulation
lessons.summary: Compare ML hardware and hosting options, summarise ML framework functions, and explain how regulation and standards affect testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Training and inference can use different hardware: a speech model may be trained in the cloud but run on a low-end phone. ML benefits from hardware that handles large data structures, massively parallel processing (for example matrix multiplication) and low-precision arithmetic (quantization, such as 4 bits instead of 32), which gives faster processing, lower power, smaller and cheaper chips and less bandwidth. CPUs offer high-precision complex operations that ML rarely needs and only a few cores. GPUs have thousands of simpler cores built for parallel graphics work, so they usually outperform CPUs for ML despite lower clock speeds, and are generally the best option for small-scale ML work. AI-specific hardware such as ASICs and System-on-a-Chip devices adds many cores, specialised data management and in-memory processing; it suits edge computing, while training happens in the cloud. Neuromorphic processors abandon the von Neumann architecture for brain-inspired designs.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A camera maker wants on-device detection of pets with long battery life, and retrains the model monthly. A sensible split is cloud GPUs (or specialised training hardware) for training, a quantized model on an AI-specific chip in the camera for inference, and tests that compare the quantized edge model with the original model, because lower precision can change predictions.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A higher clock speed does not make the CPU the better ML choice; parallelism matters more. ASICs and SoCs are typically for running models at the edge, not for training. Development (where you build and train) and hosting (where the model runs) are separate decisions, and the best answer is usually justified by size, performance, budget, security, privacy, deployment and regulation, not by a single universal rule.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which option keeps sensitive patient data under the organisation's control while still using elastic compute for heavy training? Solution: a hybrid approach, preparing private data on-premises and using cloud resources for compute-intensive work. Public cloud alone gives elasticity and pay-as-you-go pricing but less control; a private cloud gives more control at a higher upfront cost.

blocks.title: Development, hosting and frameworks
blocks.text:
AI-based systems can be bought from third parties (usually pretrained models or AI as a Service, AIaaS: faster deployment and time to market) or developed privately (better tailored, but needing specialised skills in-house or outsourced). Local development gives direct control and privacy: small models on PCs, mid-sized models on dedicated GPUs, large models on on-premises clusters with energy, cooling and hardware costs. Public clouds give pre-configured environments, pay-as-you-go pricing and easy scaling; private clouds give more security and privacy for a larger upfront investment. Hybrid approaches prototype locally, keep sensitive components such as private data preparation on-premises and use the cloud for heavy compute. Hosting ranges from local (phones, PCs: privacy, no cloud licences, limited hardware) through dedicated servers (upfront cost, control) to public cloud (scalable, no maintenance, good for fluctuating loads) and private cloud (more security and customisation at higher cost).

ML development frameworks provide data handling (loading, preprocessing, cleaning, transforming), model building (algorithm libraries, architecture, layers), training and optimisation (iteratively adjusting parameters, sometimes distributed training and fine-tuning of pretrained models), evaluation (accuracy, precision, recall for classification; error rates for ML regression) and deployment (converting models for web, mobile, edge or embedded targets). Lower-level APIs give more control but need more coding; higher-level APIs simplify work but limit customisation. Selection factors: application area, need for rapid prototyping, configurability for complex models, user expertise, deployment constraints, community support and ecosystem maturity.

blocks.title: Worked case: regulation shapes the test plan
blocks.text: A hospital deploys a triage model. Under the EU AI Act's risk-based approach, a system affecting health and safety is likely high-risk, which brings stringent requirements for rigorous testing, data governance and human oversight, with fines based on a percentage of global turnover. The test team therefore plans documented statistical testing, data provenance checks and human-oversight tests, and uses ISO/IEC TR 29119-11 for guidance on testing AI-based systems. A version of the same product sold in a country with lighter-touch regulation still benefits from these practices, but the mandatory evidence differs.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A start-up must choose a framework for a speech-recognition prototype that will later run on low-power edge devices. List four selection factors from the syllabus that apply and say which framework capability matters most for the edge target. Then explain the difference between soft law (OECD AI Principles, UN Governing AI for Humanity) and the EU AI Act.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Relevant factors: the application area (speech), the need for rapid prototyping, deployment considerations for resource-constrained environments, user expertise, community support and ecosystem maturity. The deployment capability matters most: converting the trained model into a format suitable for edge devices. Soft-law instruments are influential principles that guide governments and organisations toward human-centric, ethical AI and international cooperation, but they are not binding. The EU AI Act is binding regulation that classifies systems by risk, from minimal to unacceptable, imposes strict requirements on high-risk systems and enforces them with substantial fines.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
ML hardware needs: large data structures, massive parallelism (matrix multiplication), low-precision arithmetic (quantization: faster, less power, smaller and cheaper chips, less bandwidth). CPU: few cores, high precision, higher clock. GPU: thousands of simple cores, usually better for ML; best option for small-scale ML work. AI-specific: ASIC and System-on-a-Chip (many cores, specialised data management, in-memory processing) for edge inference; training in the cloud. Neuromorphic processors: not von Neumann, brain-inspired.
Acquire third-party (pretrained models, AIaaS: speed, time to market) or develop privately (tailored, needs skills). Development: local (control, privacy; PC → GPU → on-premises clusters), public cloud (pay-as-you-go, scaling), private cloud (security, upfront investment), hybrid. Hosting: local, dedicated servers, public cloud, private cloud, hybrid. Decision factors: model size, complexity, performance, budget, security and privacy, deployment needs, regulation.
Framework functions: data handling, model building, training and optimisation, evaluation, deployment; low- versus high-level APIs; general-purpose or specialised. Selection factors: application area, rapid prototyping, configurability, user expertise, deployment constraints, community support, ecosystem maturity.
Regulation and standards aim to make AI safe, fair, transparent, sustainable, accountable, ethical and responsibly used. OECD AI Principles and UN Governing AI for Humanity are soft law. EU AI Act: risk-based (minimal to unacceptable), high-risk systems need rigorous testing, data governance, human oversight; fines as a percentage of global turnover. ISO/IEC TR 29119-11: guidance on testing AI-based systems; ISO/IEC 42119 series in development; sector-specific rules in healthcare and finance; regulations need regular review.

lessons.title: 2.1 · AI quality characteristics and safety
lessons.summary: Classify behaviors with the ISO/IEC 25059 characteristics and explain the extra challenges of AI in safety-related systems.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: ISO/IEC 25059 extends the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model for AI-based systems, from a product-quality and a quality-in-use perspective. These characteristics shape test objectives, acceptance criteria and how results are interpreted. New or modified characteristics: AI functional correctness (product quality; a certain error rate is expected, so correctness considers correct and incorrect outputs against an acceptable threshold); functional adaptability (new sub-characteristic of functional suitability: the system autonomously adapts to changes in its operational environment after deployment); user controllability (new sub-characteristic of interaction capability, which replaces usability in ISO/IEC 25010:2023: a human or external agent can intervene in its functioning in a timely manner); transparency (sub-characteristic of interaction capability and of satisfaction: appropriate information about the system is communicated to stakeholders); AI robustness (new sub-characteristic of reliability: maintaining AI functional correctness despite biased, adversarial or invalid inputs, interference, adverse environments or operator misuse); intervenability (new sub-characteristic of security: an operator can intervene in time to prevent harm or hazard); and societal and ethical risk mitigation (quality in use, under freedom from risk: accountability, fairness and non-discrimination, privacy, safety and security, human control of technology, sustainability and more).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Classify each behavior. A navigation app re-learns traffic patterns after a new bridge opens: functional adaptability. A drone pilot takes over manual control within half a second: user controllability. A power-grid engineer vetoes a critical AI action before it executes to prevent a blackout: intervenability (the focus is preventing harm). A model keeps its accuracy when one sensor feeds noisy values: AI robustness. A dashboard shows the deployed model version and links to its documentation: transparency.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: User controllability and intervenability both involve human intervention. User controllability (interaction capability) is about a user or external agent being able to intervene in a timely manner during normal operation; intervenability (security) is specifically about an operator intervening in time to prevent harm or hazard. Transparency is not the same as explainability: transparency is about communicating appropriate information (such as version, provenance, documentation) to stakeholders.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which characteristic does this measure address: 'the percentage of correct object classifications when the camera lens is partly covered by rain'? Solution: AI robustness, because it measures whether AI functional correctness is maintained under adverse environmental conditions. If the measure were simply 'accuracy on the standard test set', it would address AI functional correctness.

blocks.title: AI and safety
blocks.text: Safety-related systems can harm people, property or the environment. Testing them is already demanding; AI adds five challenges. Specifications: requirements often begin as vague goals that are implicitly provided via training data, so traceability from requirements to implementation can be inadequate. Non-determinism: random number generation or tiny input variations can produce unexpected behavior even after rigorous testing. Self-learning: behavior drifts away from the tested behavior after deployment; managing how and from what the model learns, or adding safety guards (such as a content-moderation component that filters prompts), can help. Explainability and transparency: decisions are hard to understand; explainable-AI techniques such as LIME can give insight but are not widely available and may cost performance. Evolving regulations: mature functional safety standards do not yet include AI and some prohibit it, while the EU AI Act classifies AI safety components (aviation, medical devices, automotive) as high-risk with strict development and testing requirements.

blocks.title: Worked case: a self-learning safety function
blocks.text: A factory robot uses a model that keeps learning from operator corrections. The original safety case was built from pre-deployment tests. After six months of learning, the tested behavior no longer describes the deployed behavior, so the safety integrity argument is undermined. Mitigations: restrict what and how the model learns, add a non-AI safety guard that stops motion outside a certified envelope, monitor behavior continuously, and re-test after significant learning updates.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: For each statement, name the safety challenge: (1) the requirement says 'drive safely' and the rest is implied by labelled driving data; (2) two identical runs give different braking points because of random initialisation; (3) a medical regulator asks why the model recommended surgery; (4) a functional safety standard used by the project does not allow ML components.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Specifications: vague goals implicitly encoded in training data weaken traceability. (2) Non-determinism. (3) Explainability and transparency; an explainable-AI technique such as LIME may help. (4) Evolving regulations: mature functional safety standards do not include, or even prohibit, AI.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Chapter 2 keywords: functional adaptability, AI functional correctness, intervenability, AI robustness, safety, societal and ethical risk mitigation, transparency, user controllability.
ISO/IEC 25059 extends ISO/IEC 25010 with two perspectives: product quality and quality in use. Parent characteristics: functional adaptability → functional suitability; user controllability → interaction capability (replaced usability in the 2023 edition of 25010); transparency → interaction capability and satisfaction (quality in use); AI robustness → reliability; intervenability → security; societal and ethical risk mitigation → freedom from risk (quality in use); AI functional correctness → product quality, defined with acceptable thresholds for incorrect results.
Safety challenges: specifications, non-determinism, self-learning (mitigate with managed learning and safety guards), explainability and transparency (explainable AI such as LIME: limited availability, possible performance cost), evolving regulations (functional safety standards exclude or prohibit AI; EU AI Act: safety components are high-risk).

lessons.title: 2.2 · Acceptance criteria for AI-based systems
lessons.summary: Write measurable, often statistical or threshold-based, acceptance criteria for each AI quality characteristic and safety.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Acceptance criteria for AI-based systems should cover functional and non-functional characteristics. For AI-specific characteristics they are often statistical, probabilistic or threshold-based rather than binary, which makes testing harder: you need enough tests to show a threshold is met. A good criterion names the characteristic, a measurable quantity, a threshold and the conditions under which it applies.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: AI functional correctness: 'recall of at least 90% on the defect-prediction test set'. Functional adaptability: 'after a user watches three documentaries in one session, at least 40% of homepage recommendations are documentaries'. User controllability: 'a supervisor can take control of the drone within 0.5 s of a GPS-loss distress signal'. Transparency: 'the API returns the deployed model's unique version identifier and a link to its documentation'. AI robustness: 'prediction response time stays below 1 s while the central database is unavailable for 30 s'. Intervenability: 'an engineer has a 30-second window to veto any critical action before it executes'. Societal and ethical risk mitigation: 'the chatbot scores at least 95% in an internal red-teaming assessment for refusing violent, self-harm or hateful content'. Safety: 'non-AI components of the steering system comply with ISO 26262-6 at ASIL C'.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A criterion such as 'the system is easy to configure' describes ordinary usability, not an ISO/IEC 25059 AI-specific characteristic, and it is not measurable as written. Watch for criteria that use AI vocabulary but cannot be checked (no threshold, no conditions), and for criteria assigned to the wrong characteristic.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Rewrite 'the model should be fair' as an acceptance criterion. Solution: 'For loan decisions, the approval-rate difference between gender groups is within the agreed fairness metric threshold on the representative evaluation dataset.' It names the characteristic (societal and ethical risk mitigation: fairness), a metric, a threshold and conditions.

blocks.title: Statistical criteria and conditions
blocks.text: Because outputs are probabilistic, an AI criterion usually needs a sample: '95% accuracy' only means something when tested on a sufficiently large, representative dataset (see 6.1.3 for margins of error and confidence levels). Time-based criteria (adapt within 20 s, intervene within 0.5 s, regulate within 0.15 s) need a defined trigger and measurement point. Robustness criteria name the adverse condition explicitly (temperature above 85 °C for 10 s, database outage for 30 s). Safety criteria may combine AI-specific evidence, such as explainability-tool mapping accuracy, with conventional functional safety compliance for non-AI parts.

blocks.title: Worked case: an edge device under heat
blocks.text: An edge camera must not crash in hot conditions. Criterion: 'when internal temperature exceeds 85 °C for a continuous 10 s, the device switches automatically to a lower-fidelity, reduced-power inference mode'. Characteristic: AI robustness. Test: hold the device in a climate chamber above 85 °C, observe the mode change after 10 s, and check that predictions continue rather than failing.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Write one acceptance criterion each for functional adaptability of an engine-management system, intervenability of a production-line robot and transparency of a third-party model. Include a threshold or a verifiable condition in each.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Functional adaptability: 'when the vehicle crosses the specified altitude threshold, the engine-management system adapts within 20 seconds'. Intervenability: 'if the robot breaches its safety zone, the production line shuts down within 0.5 s of a shutdown being initiated'. Transparency: 'sufficient information about the third-party model and the provenance of its training data is provided to meet the relevant company standard'. Each is verifiable because it states a trigger and a measurable outcome or a reference standard.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Acceptance criteria cover AI functional correctness (accuracy, recall thresholds), functional adaptability (time to adapt, change in recommendations), user controllability (time to take control, notification and manual override thresholds), transparency (provenance information, version identifier and documentation endpoint), AI robustness (latency under disruption, safe degraded mode), intervenability (safety-zone shutdown time, veto window), societal and ethical risk mitigation (fairness metric, red-teaming score) and safety (ISO 26262-6 ASIL compliance for non-AI parts, explainability mapping accuracy, regulation of out-of-limit control signals within a time).
AI criteria are often statistical, probabilistic or threshold-based, not binary.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Forms of ML, the ML workflow, and adapting pretrained models
lessons.summary: Distinguish supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, summarise the ML workflow and compare fine-tuning with RAG.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Supervised learning trains on labelled data (inputs with known outputs). Classification assigns inputs to predefined classes (spam or not spam, image recognition). ML regression predicts continuous values (age from lifestyle data, stock prices); note that 'ML regression' is not the regression of other ISTQB syllabi, which means change-related defects. Unsupervised learning trains on unlabelled data: clustering groups similar data points (customer segments) and association finds relationships between attributes (purchase patterns used for recommendations). Reinforcement learning uses an intelligent agent that interacts with an environment and receives rewards or penalties; its challenges are setting up the environment, designing the reward function and choosing a strategy. Typical uses are robotics, autonomous vehicles and adaptive systems such as chatbots.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Predict next month's energy demand in kWh from past data: supervised learning, ML regression. Label incoming tickets as 'billing', 'technical' or 'other' using a labelled history: classification. Group sensors whose readings behave alike without any labels: clustering. Find that customers who buy tents often buy headlamps: association. Teach a warehouse robot to move faster by rewarding completed picks and penalising collisions: reinforcement learning.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not confuse 'predicts a number' (ML regression) with 'predicts a category' (classification), even if the category is numerically coded. Reinforcement learning does not learn from a fixed labelled dataset; it learns from feedback on its own actions. And a model that improves by searching the internet for examples is not, on that basis alone, reinforcement learning.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A model predicts whether a machine will fail within 7 days (yes or no) from sensor data and maintenance records. Which form? Solution: supervised classification. If it predicted the number of hours until failure, it would be ML regression.

blocks.title: The ML workflow
blocks.text:
The workflow is: understand the objectives (stakeholders agree the purpose and acceptance criteria, including ML functional performance metrics); select a framework; select and build the algorithm (often from a library); prepare and test data (acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering, possibly exploratory data analysis, plus testing of the data and automated preparation steps); train the model (model hyperparameters define the structure, such as layers or tree depth; algorithm hyperparameters control training, such as the number of iterations); evaluate the model on the validation dataset against agreed metrics; tune the model by adjusting hyperparameters and retraining; test the model with an independent test dataset to confirm the acceptance criteria and compare with evaluation results; deploy the model (re-engineer it with its data pipeline for the target platform and test it again); use the model (batch or real-time predictions inside a larger system); and monitor and tune it for drift, retraining if necessary and comparing new and old models with A/B testing. Training, evaluation and tuning together form 'model generation'. The workflow is iterative, and integration with non-ML components is extra work at integration, system and acceptance test levels.

Fine-tuning takes a pretrained neural network and trains it further on task-specific data; it needs far less data and effort than training from scratch. It can update all layers, only some (usually near the output) or added layers, and works best when the new task resembles the original. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) instead gives an LLM task-specific data sources converted into a searchable form; relevant documents are retrieved and added to an enhanced prompt, so the pretrained model itself is unchanged. RAG and fine-tuning can be combined. Biases and vulnerabilities of the pretrained model typically carry over, so the adapted model must be tested.

blocks.title: Worked case: evaluation is not testing
blocks.text: A team reports 94% accuracy and wants to deploy. Ask which dataset produced it. If it came from the validation dataset used to tune the hyperparameters, it is an evaluation result and is optimistically biased. The 'test the model' activity needs an independent test dataset. If the test accuracy is much lower (say 85%), the team should return to model generation, or even to data preparation.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Place each activity in the workflow: (1) choosing the number of hidden layers; (2) setting the number of training epochs; (3) checking a converted model on the target phone; (4) agreeing that recall must reach 90%; (5) comparing a retrained model with the live model; (6) measuring F1 on validation data and adjusting the learning rate.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Train the model: a model hyperparameter passed to the algorithm. (2) Train the model: an algorithm hyperparameter. (3) Deploy the model: the re-engineered model is tested on its platform. (4) Understand the objectives: acceptance criteria. (5) Monitor and tune the model: a form of A/B testing. (6) Evaluate and tune the model (model generation).

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-3.1.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Using any ML development framework or spreadsheet tool, train a simple classifier (for example a decision tree) on a labelled dataset, keep a validation split for tuning and a separate test split. Compare validation accuracy with test accuracy and write two sentences explaining why evaluation/tuning and testing are different activities.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Data preparation and datasets
lessons.summary: Explain data acquisition, preprocessing and feature engineering, and contrast training, validation and test datasets including k-fold cross-validation.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Data preparation is one of the most crucial and resource-intensive activities in the ML workflow, typically consuming more effort than model selection and building. It is closely linked to the data pipeline, which turns raw data into a usable format for both training and prediction. If operational data differs significantly from training data, performance and safety assumptions may not hold. Data preparation has three groups of activities. Data acquisition: identify relevant data types (numerical, categorical, images, text and more), gather data from databases, APIs or sensors, and label data for supervised learning while checking accuracy and consistency. Data preprocessing: clean the data (remove defects, duplicates and outliers; impute missing values with mean, median or mode; anonymise or remove personal information), transform formats, scale and normalise, augment the data (more samples, adversarial examples for robustness, synthetic data) and sample subsets to cut training time and cost. Feature engineering: select features by their contribution to performance and extract a smaller set of informative, non-redundant features. Exploratory data analysis (EDA) runs alongside: discovering trends, patterns and anomalies and visualising data with plots and charts.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A churn dataset has 2% missing ages, 300 duplicate customer rows, a free-text 'notes' column with phone numbers, and income values from 0 to 2,000,000. Preparation: remove duplicates; impute ages with the median; remove or mask phone numbers for privacy; review extreme incomes as possible outliers; scale income; and check with EDA histograms whether churners are rare enough to need augmentation or resampling.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Augmentation adds examples; sampling reduces the number of examples. Feature engineering happens during data preparation, before training, not after deployment. EDA is an analysis activity running in parallel with preparation, not a form of exploratory testing of the model.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which activity is 'replacing missing blood-pressure values with the median of the column'? Solution: data preprocessing (cleaning: imputing missing values). Which is 'keeping only the 12 features that most improve validation F1'? Feature engineering (feature selection).

blocks.title: Training, validation and test datasets
blocks.text: Logically, three equivalent datasets are needed, for example randomly selected from one representative dataset: the training dataset trains the model; the validation dataset evaluates it and guides tuning; the test dataset (also called the holdout dataset) tests the tuned model. With plenty of data, the split sizes depend on model complexity, the training algorithm, available resources (memory, disk, compute, bandwidth, time) and the desired confidence in the model. With limited data, a three-way split can leave too little training data and increase the risk of underfitting. A common strategy is to set aside a small final hold-out test set and use k-fold cross-validation (k commonly 5 or 10) on the rest: the data is divided into k folds; each fold serves once as the validation set while the model trains on the other k−1; metrics are averaged across folds to estimate generalisation and tune hyperparameters; the final model is then trained on all training-plus-validation data and tested once on the hold-out set. Stratified sampling keeps each fold representative, especially with imbalanced data. Without any hold-out set, the averaged cross-validation result is optimistically biased and is not an unbiased estimate. Other resampling methods are leave-one-out cross-validation (k equals the number of samples) and bootstrap techniques.

blocks.title: Worked case: a small medical dataset
blocks.text: A team has 1,200 labelled scans. Instead of a 60/20/20 split, they reserve 150 scans as a final hold-out test set, run 5-fold cross-validation on the remaining 1,050 (each fold of 210 scans validates once), average the F1-scores to choose hyperparameters, retrain on all 1,050 and test once on the 150 scans. Reporting the cross-validation average as the final result would be optimistically biased.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A dataset of 900 records is used for 10-fold cross-validation with no separate hold-out set. (1) How many records validate in each fold? (2) How many models are trained during cross-validation? (3) Can the averaged validation score be reported as an unbiased estimate of operational performance?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) 90 records per fold. (2) Ten models, one per fold, each trained on 810 records. (3) No. Without a hold-out test set the average is optimistically biased because the same data guided tuning; it cannot serve as an unbiased estimate.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-3.2.2)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Take a small tabular dataset and perform the applicable preparation steps: identify data types, remove duplicates, impute missing values, remove personal data, scale numeric features and split the data. Keep a short log of each step: you will reuse the prepared data when you calculate metrics in section 3.3.

blocks.text:
Data acquisition: identify data types, gather from diverse sources (databases, APIs, real-time sensors), label for supervised learning. Data forms: numerical, categorical, image, tabular, text, time series, sensor, geospatial, video, audio.
Data preprocessing: cleaning (defects, duplicates, outliers; impute with mean/median/mode; anonymise or remove personal information), transforming formats, scaling and normalising, augmenting (more samples, adversarial examples, synthetic data), sampling subsets.
Feature engineering: feature selection and feature extraction (informative, non-redundant subset). EDA in parallel: trends, patterns, anomalies; visualisation.
Preparation is iterative, often manual; activities may be reordered or omitted. Operational data should match training data characteristics (distributions, feature ranges); production preparation steps may be adjusted for efficiency.
Datasets: training (train), validation (evaluate and tune), test/holdout (test the tuned model). Split factors: model complexity, algorithm, resources, desired confidence. Limited data: small hold-out set plus k-fold cross-validation (k usually 5 or 10), stratified sampling, average the fold metrics, retrain on the full pool, test once on hold-out; without hold-out the CV average is optimistically biased. Also leave-one-out CV and bootstrap.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Calculating ML functional performance metrics
lessons.summary: Build a confusion matrix and calculate accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score for a classifier (K3).

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text:
In a classification problem a model rarely predicts every case correctly, partly because ML models are probabilistic and data is noisy. A confusion matrix counts four outcomes. True positive (TP): predicted positive and actually positive. False positive (FP): predicted positive but actually negative. False negative (FN): predicted negative but actually positive. True negative (TN): predicted negative and actually negative. The matrix may be drawn with predicted and actual swapped, so always read the labels before calculating. The metrics:
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) × 100%: the percentage of all classifications that are correct.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) × 100%: of the positive predictions, how many were right; how sure you can be about a positive prediction.
Recall (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN) × 100%: of the actual positives, how many were found; how confident you can be that positives are not missed.
F1-score = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall): the harmonic mean of precision and recall, from 0 to 100. Close to 100 means both are high; a low F1 means the model misses true cases, raises false alarms, or both.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text:
A fraud model is tested on 1,000 transactions: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 930.
Accuracy = (40 + 930) / 1,000 = 97.0%.
Precision = 40 / (40 + 10) = 80.0%.
Recall = 40 / (40 + 20) = 66.7%.
F1 = 2 × 80.0 × 66.7 / (80.0 + 66.7) = 72.7.
High accuracy hides the weakness: one fraud case in three is missed. Imbalanced data makes accuracy look good because negatives dominate.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Precision divides by predicted positives (TP + FP); recall divides by actual positives (TP + FN). Mixing the two denominators is the most common error. F1 is not the arithmetic mean: for precision 90 and recall 50, the mean is 70 but F1 is 2 × 90 × 50 / 140 = 64.3. Also check whether the question gives the matrix as predicted-by-actual or actual-by-predicted.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A spam filter: TP = 45, FP = 5, FN = 15, TN = 135. Calculate the four metrics. Solution: total 200; accuracy = 180 / 200 = 90.0%; precision = 45 / 50 = 90.0%; recall = 45 / 60 = 75.0%; F1 = 2 × 90 × 75 / 165 = 81.8.

blocks.title: Choosing and interpreting the metric
blocks.text: Choose the metric that matches the cost of each error. When false negatives are dangerous (a missed tumour, a missed defect, undetected fraud), recall matters most. When false positives are expensive (blocking legitimate payments, sending a healthy patient to surgery), precision matters most. F1 balances both when both errors matter and positives are rare. Accuracy is informative only when classes are reasonably balanced and both error types cost about the same. Acceptance criteria (section 2.2) often state a threshold for one of these metrics, and ML functional performance testing (section 6.1.3) checks the threshold statistically on a large, representative test dataset.

blocks.title: Worked case: comparing two models
blocks.text:
Two defect-prediction models are tested on 500 modules containing 100 defective ones. Model X: TP 80, FP 40, FN 20, TN 360. Model Y: TP 70, FP 10, FN 30, TN 390.
X: accuracy 88.0%, precision 66.7%, recall 80.0%, F1 72.7. Y: accuracy 92.0%, precision 87.5%, recall 70.0%, F1 77.8.
If the acceptance criterion is 'recall of at least 75%' (missing defective modules is costly), X meets it and Y does not, even though Y has better accuracy and F1.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: An image classifier for cracked welds is tested on 400 images: 60 are cracked. It flags 75 images as cracked, of which 54 really are cracked. Build the confusion matrix and calculate accuracy, precision, recall and F1.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-3.3.2 and HO-3.3.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Using the classifier from section 3.1, calculate and display accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with your framework's library functions and check one value by hand from the confusion matrix. Then train different models (for example a decision tree and a logistic regression) on different dataset combinations and compare training times and metrics.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text: Confusion matrix cells: TP, FP, FN, TN; orientation may differ but the four situations are the same. Accuracy = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)×100%. Precision = TP/(TP+FP)×100%. Recall (sensitivity) = TP/(TP+FN)×100%. F1 = 2×(P×R)/(P+R), harmonic mean, 0-100. These metrics measure classification quality and reveal a model's strengths and weaknesses; ML functional performance criteria are thresholds on such metrics agreed in the objectives.

lessons.title: 3.4 · Neural networks and neural-network coverage
lessons.summary: Explain how a deep neural network computes and learns, and describe neuron, k-multisection and neuron boundary coverage.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Artificial neural networks were inspired by biological neurons. The single-layer perceptron is an early network with one layer; it learns binary classifiers for linearly separable problems by drawing a straight-line boundary in input space. Most current networks are deep neural networks (DNN) with several layers; fully connected networks can be seen as multi-layer perceptrons. A DNN has an input layer (for example camera pixel values), hidden layers of artificial neurons (nodes) and an output layer (for example the likelihood that an image shows a cat). In fully connected architectures each neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each neuron after the input layer computes an activation value: a weighted sum of the activation values of connected neurons in the previous layer, plus the neuron's own bias, passed through a non-linear activation function. This bias is a model parameter, unrelated to unfair bias in data (section 5.1.2).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A neuron receives activations 0.5 and 0.2 through weights 0.8 and −0.5, and has bias 0.1. Weighted sum = 0.5 × 0.8 + 0.2 × (−0.5) + 0.1 = 0.4 − 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4. With a ReLU activation (max(0, x)) the activation value is 0.4; a different activation function would give a different value.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Weights belong to connections; biases belong to neurons. Training does not write rules into the network; it adjusts weights and biases to reduce the loss. An epoch is one pass through the whole training dataset, not one training example. High neuron coverage does not show that a network generalises well: it can activate the right neurons for the wrong reasons (spurious correlations).

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Put the training steps in order: compare output with the correct result; initialise weights and biases with small random values; feed training data forward through the activation functions; feed the error back to adjust weights and biases; repeat over epochs. Solution: initialise; feed forward; compare (loss); feed the error back and adjust; repeat until the output is good enough.

blocks.title: Coverage measures for neural networks
blocks.text: Neural networks do not follow explicitly coded paths, so statement or branch coverage says little about them. Structural coverage measures instead assess how thoroughly test inputs exercise the network's internals. Neuron coverage: the proportion of neurons whose output exceeds a specified threshold during testing. k-multisection neuron coverage (kMNC): each neuron's possible output range is divided into k sections, and kMNC is the proportion of all these sections activated during testing. Neuron boundary coverage (NBC): the proportion of neurons whose output during testing goes above the maximum or below the minimum observed in training. These measures reveal parts of the model that remain untested and so help testers design extra inputs, but commercial tool support is limited and structural coverage does not guarantee generalisation, so testers should also use adversarial and metamorphic testing.

blocks.title: Worked case: interpreting coverage
blocks.text: A network has 200 hidden neurons. With threshold 0.5, 150 neurons exceed it for at least one test input: neuron coverage = 75%. With k = 4 there are 800 sections, of which 360 were activated: kMNC = 45%. Only 6 neurons produced outputs outside their training range: NBC = 3%. Low NBC means the tests rarely push neurons beyond trained behavior, a hint to add unusual or boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A network has 50 neurons and testing uses a threshold of 0.3. 35 neurons exceed the threshold for some test input. Each neuron's range is split into 5 sections and 110 sections were reached. 4 neurons exceeded their training maximum and 1 fell below its training minimum. Calculate neuron coverage, kMNC and NBC, then name one limitation of all three.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Neuron coverage = 35 / 50 = 70%. kMNC = 110 / (50 × 5) = 110 / 250 = 44%. NBC = (4 + 1) / 50 = 10%. Limitation: none of them shows that the network generalises or that activations happen for the right reasons; they guide additional test design but must be combined with other techniques.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-3.4.2)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. In a spreadsheet, train a perceptron with two inputs and a bias to learn the AND function. Start with small weights, apply the update rule after each example and continue epoch by epoch until all four input combinations are classified correctly and the error is zero.

blocks.text:
Perceptron: single layer, binary classifier, linearly separable problems. DNN: input, hidden and output layers; neurons (nodes); fully connected networks resemble multi-layer perceptrons. Activation value = activation function(weighted sum of previous activations + neuron bias). Training: weights and biases initialised small and random (biases sometimes zero), feed forward, compare output with correct result to get the error (loss), feed back to adjust weights and biases, repeat over epochs until good enough.
Coverage: neuron coverage (output above a threshold), kMNC (k sections of each neuron's output range), NBC (output above training maximum or below training minimum). Benefits: reveal untested areas, guide new test inputs. Limits: few commercial tools, no guarantee of generalisation (spurious correlations); combine with adversarial and metamorphic testing.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Locked versus adaptive systems, statistics and test oracles
lessons.summary: Compare testability of locked and adaptive systems, justify statistical testing and address the test oracle problem.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A locked AI-based system does not change its behavior after deployment: a DNN whose weights and biases are fixed until it is retrained, such as lane detection or traffic-sign recognition in safety-related driving functions. An adaptive AI-based system, such as a reinforcement learning system, changes its behavior after deployment based on a reward function or a new operational environment, in ways that cannot be predicted in advance, such as an e-commerce recommender learning evolving preferences. Many GenAI chatbots are locked at runtime but updated periodically, so they sit between the extremes; real systems span a continuum. Locked systems are far easier to test because they are largely deterministic and expected results do not change; an updated locked system is treated as a new system needing a fresh round of testing. Even locked systems can show non-determinism from floating-point limits and parallel GPU execution. Adaptive systems can be tested before deployment (simulated environment changes, testing the learning mechanism, controlled adaptation scenarios), but the system may change during or because of testing, and unpredictable new behaviors cannot have test cases prepared. Practical responses: an automated suite focused on core functionality run after significant changes, and checks that performance has not degraded beyond a threshold, both after changes and as ongoing monitoring.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A bank's credit model is retrained quarterly and frozen in between: it is locked during each quarter, and each retrained version needs a full new round of testing. A game opponent that learns from every match is adaptive: the team runs a core-behavior regression suite nightly and monitors win-rate degradation thresholds, because they cannot predict which strategies it will learn next.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: 'Locked' does not mean 'never updated'; it means behavior does not change during operation between updates. A locked model can still be slightly non-deterministic on GPUs. And testing an adaptive system thoroughly before deployment is possible, but it cannot cover behaviors that the system has not yet learned.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Why is a single failed test (a cat classified as a dog) not enough to judge an image model? Solution: the model is probabilistic, so one result does not reflect its overall AI functional correctness; a statistically significant number of tests, sampled from the operational data distribution, is needed.

blocks.title: Statistical testing and test oracles
blocks.text:
A statistical approach is needed because of non-determinism (the same input may give different outputs, so the suite must be large enough for statistically significant results), distributional performance evaluation (training data never exactly matches operational data, so a statistically significant sample of operational scenarios must be tested), handling uncertainty and bias (confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and error analysis quantify accuracy, fairness and robustness) and regulatory and safety contexts (claims must hold with high confidence across many scenarios).

The test oracle problem, deciding whether an output is correct, is harder for AI because of probabilistic and non-deterministic outputs (pass/fail needs thresholds or tolerances), exploratory development with incomplete or missing specifications, task complexity beyond straightforward human checking, subjective behavior (expectations of a virtual assistant vary) and self-learning (yesterday's expected result may no longer be correct). Ways to address it: defining output boundaries (acceptable ranges, distributions, limits and tolerances, such as a maximum stopping distance); defining environmental boundaries (fix lighting, temperature or latency so outputs are repeatable); expert consultation (helpful but experts can disagree or be wrong); specialised testing such as A/B, back-to-back and metamorphic testing, which compare behaviors or check properties without explicit expected results; and proxy oracles (secondary systems or models, including other AI, that assess outputs).

blocks.title: Worked case: an autonomous shuttle
blocks.text: Expected results for 'brake for a pedestrian' cannot be a single exact stopping point. The team defines an output boundary (stop at least 2 m before the pedestrian), fixes environmental boundaries for each run (dry road, daylight, 30 km/h), runs hundreds of trials to measure the proportion within the boundary with a confidence level, and asks road-safety experts to review edge cases such as partly hidden pedestrians.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Match each oracle approach to a situation: output boundaries, environmental boundaries, expert consultation, metamorphic testing, proxy oracle. (1) A dermatologist judges whether a lesion classification is plausible. (2) A second model trained on labelled data scores an unlabelled test set. (3) Search results must still contain the same top documents when a synonym is used. (4) Tests run at a fixed network latency of 50 ms. (5) Delivery-time estimates must fall within ±10 minutes of the actual time.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Expert consultation. (2) Proxy oracle. (3) Metamorphic testing (a relation between source and follow-up outputs). (4) Environmental boundaries. (5) Output boundaries (tolerance).

Chapter 4 keywords: attack, exploratory testing, risk-based testing, test oracle. AI-specific keywords: adaptive AI-based system, AI-based system, generative AI, large language model, locked AI-based system.
Locked: fixed post-deployment behavior, mostly deterministic, easier to test, updated version = new system to retest; possible floating-point/GPU non-determinism. Adaptive: changes after deployment (reward function, environment), unpredictable; test before deployment by simulation, testing the learning mechanism, controlled scenarios; core-functionality automated suite after significant changes; degradation thresholds, ongoing monitoring. GenAI chatbots: locked at runtime, updated periodically.
Statistical approach reasons: non-determinism, distributional performance evaluation, handling uncertainty and bias (confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, error analysis), regulatory and safety context.
Oracle difficulties: probabilistic/non-deterministic, exploratory development and incomplete specifications, task complexity, subjectivity, self-learning. Solutions: output boundaries, environmental boundaries, expert consultation, specialised testing (A/B, back-to-back, metamorphic), proxy oracles; also statistical evaluation and a defined ground truth.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Testing generative AI and red teaming
lessons.summary: Explain how GenAI systems are tested and apply a red-teaming approach to a GenAI system (K3).

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Testing GenAI evaluates the correctness, coherence and creativity of outputs (including originality and novelty) and checks functional and non-functional requirements, adapting strategies to text, image, video and audio content. Black-box testing is common: testers supply prompts, images or partial data and assess clarity, originality and adherence to domain rules; it suits end-user applications such as chatbots or design tools whose value depends on useful, plausible content. The input explosion problem makes this hard: optional system prompts plus user prompts that can carry large and varied data, API access, parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and the context window that keeps earlier conversation all influence the output. Pass/fail may need manual review against qualitative criteria, or a second GenAI system can judge outputs automatically (an image-recognition model checking a generated image), used carefully because it may share biases or errors. Non-functional testing matters as much: resource use in inference and training (CPU and GPU load, memory, network bandwidth) and response times. Benchmark suites are curated datasets and tasks that give standardised, reproducible comparisons of language understanding, reasoning or coding ability.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A customer-support chatbot is tested with a fixed system prompt, temperature 0.2 and a 20-turn conversation. The tester varies the user prompt (short, long with a pasted contract, multilingual), checks answers for correctness and adherence to the refund policy, uses a second LLM to score politeness on 500 transcripts while sampling its judgements manually, measures response time and GPU memory, and compares the release candidate with the previous version on a public reasoning benchmark.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Red teaming is not the same as benchmarking. Benchmarks are static and standardised; red teaming is adaptive and dynamic, with prompts changed immediately in response to outputs, to drive the system into harmful or undesirable behavior. Red teaming is proactive and pre-deployment; blue teaming is the ongoing, real-time defensive monitoring and filtering of an operational system.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Name three input factors that cause the input explosion problem for an LLM application. Solution: any three of system prompt, user prompt content (potentially very large), API parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and the context window carrying earlier conversation.

blocks.title: Red teaming in practice
blocks.text:
Red teaming (RT) is a systematic, often black-box form of fault attack that probes an AI-based system for harmful capabilities, especially in its outputs, by deliberately trying to make it produce harmful or undesirable results: privacy violations, racist views, guidance for chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) attacks. Findings are used to strengthen the system. It is especially important for GenAI because the input and output spaces create a huge attack space. RT usually covers the end-to-end system but can target only the model. Beyond security and safety, it can look for problems with reliability, privacy, fairness, bias and misinformation, and it is increasingly expected by regulation such as the EU AI Act. Security RT looks for external attack vulnerabilities, including AI-specific ones such as indirect prompt injection and malicious content hidden in documents retrieved by RAG; safety RT often looks for harmful outputs under ordinary, non-adversarial use, such as unsafe medical advice.

RT is most effective before deployment but after initial internal quality checks. The core activity is interactive prompting, often multi-turn dialogues of 15-20 turns. The approach: (1) assemble a diverse team covering many perspectives and attack vectors; (2) provide access to the system in a safe test environment; (3) prompt the system to find vulnerabilities by open-ended exploration or checklists; (4) analyse the failures to understand threats; (5) create datasets from these threats to support mitigations and improvements. Coverage can be extended with crowd-sourced prompts, automated generation of attack prompts by one LLM with outputs checked by another, or hybrid human-plus-automation approaches. Insights feed blue-team monitoring and filters.

blocks.title: Worked case: red-teaming a pharmacy assistant
blocks.text: Before launch, a pharmacy chatbot that uses RAG over drug leaflets is red-teamed. The team includes a pharmacist, a security tester, a privacy specialist and testers from different cultural backgrounds. In an isolated environment they run multi-turn conversations, for example slowly steering from dosage questions toward lethal doses, and try a leaflet document containing hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection). They log each failure, analyse which policy it breaks, and turn the successful attack prompts into a dataset used to train filters and as a regression test set. Live-traffic filtering after launch is blue teaming.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A legal-advice LLM will be released next month. Order the following red-teaming steps and add the missing one: analyse failures to understand threats; give the team access in a safe environment; build a dataset from the threats for mitigation; prompt the system with exploratory and checklist-based attacks.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Missing first step: assemble a diverse team covering a wide range of perspectives and attack vectors. Order: assemble the team; provide access in a safe test environment; prompt to find vulnerabilities (open exploration or checklists, often 15-20-turn dialogues); analyse failures to understand threats; create datasets from the threats to support mitigations and improvements.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-4.2.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Run a timed exploratory session in which you ask an LLM to generate test cases for an input field using 2-value and then 3-value boundary value analysis. Record your charter, prompts and observations on a session sheet, then debrief: check every generated value against the correct boundary sets and note missing or wrong values.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
GenAI testing evaluates correctness, coherence, creativity (originality, novelty) and functional and non-functional requirements across text, image, video and audio. Black-box testing with varied inputs; clarity, originality, domain rules. Input explosion: system and user prompts, API access, parameters (temperature, maximum tokens), context window. Oracles: manual review against qualitative criteria or a second GenAI system (risk of shared biases). Non-functional: CPU/GPU usage, memory, network bandwidth, response times in inference and training. Benchmark suites: standardised, reproducible comparison.
Red teaming: systematic, often black-box fault attack (from military wargaming and NASA tiger teams) to elicit harmful outputs (privacy violations, racist views, CBRN guidance); end-to-end or model only; areas include security, safety, reliability, privacy, fairness, bias, misinformation; regulatory expectation (EU AI Act); adaptive and dynamic, complements benchmarking. Security RT: indirect prompt injection, malicious content in RAG documents. Safety RT: harmful outputs under ordinary use. Timing: before deployment, after internal quality assessment. Interactive multi-turn prompting (15-20 turns). Steps: diverse team, safe environment, prompting (exploration or checklists), failure analysis, datasets for mitigation. Scale: crowd-sourcing, LLM-generated attacks checked by another LLM, hybrid. Blue teaming: ongoing real-time defensive monitoring and filtering.

lessons.title: 4.3 · Test levels and risk-based testing for ML systems
lessons.summary: Summarise the ML-specific and conventional test levels and explain risk-based testing of ML systems.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Non-AI components of a machine learning system (MLS) are tested with conventional test levels, but ML adds two specialised test levels. Input data testing (chapter 5) covers the training data used to train the model and the production data used to make predictions in operation. ML model testing (chapter 6) covers the ML model, the ultimate output of the ML workflow. These do not cover every ML risk, so conventional levels are still needed depending on risk. Component testing: non-AI components such as the user interface, data pipeline and communication components. Component integration testing: inputs from the data pipeline arrive as the model expects, and predictions are passed to and used correctly by other components such as the UI; when AI is provided as a service, API testing of that service belongs here. System testing: confirmation testing that the ML functional performance measured in model testing is not harmed once the model is embedded in the complete system, especially after deliberate changes such as compressing a DNN, plus non-functional tests such as end-to-end prediction time. System integration testing: interfaces and data exchanges with external systems in an operationally representative environment. Acceptance testing: when AI is used as a service, whether the service suits the intended system and meets ML functional performance criteria.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A mobile app sends photos to a cloud plant-identification API. Input data testing checks the training images and the photos the app sends. Model testing checks the identification model. Component integration testing checks that the app resizes photos as the API expects and displays the returned species correctly, including API tests of the service. System testing confirms that accuracy measured on the model alone still holds through the whole app, and measures response time. Acceptance testing decides whether the purchased API meets the agreed accuracy criterion.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: The two ML-specific test levels are input data testing and ML model testing, not 'training testing' and 'deployment testing'. API testing of an AI service is part of component integration testing. System testing after model compression is confirmation testing of ML functional performance, not merely smoke testing.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A DNN is pruned to fit on a car's control unit. At which level do you confirm that its accuracy is still acceptable inside the vehicle software? Solution: system testing, as confirmation testing that the ML functional performance from model testing is not adversely affected once the changed model is embedded.

blocks.title: Risk-based testing of ML systems
blocks.text: Risk-based testing applies to all systems, and most AI regulations require a risk-based approach. ML risks include project risks (about developing the MLS) and product risks (about the MLS itself). One categorisation follows the ML workflow. Development: the algorithm, model development and framework, with example project risks such as sub-optimal algorithm selection, poor choice of evaluation approach and framework security vulnerabilities (chapter 7). Input data: training and production data, with product risks such as biased training data, data-pipeline defects and unrepresentative training data (chapter 5). Model: the generated model, with product risks such as failure to reach required ML functional performance, overfitting and susceptibility to adversarial examples (chapter 6). Another categorisation uses the ISO/IEC 25059 quality characteristics. ML-specific test approaches such as data pipeline testing, adversarial testing and algorithm/model suitability reviews mitigate these risks.

blocks.title: Worked case: a hiring-screening model
blocks.text: Risks identified: the training data reflects historical hiring skews (input data, product risk → testing for bias, data representativeness testing); the team picked an algorithm because it was familiar, not suitable (development, project risk → algorithm suitability review, A/B comparison); the model scores CVs with unusual formatting unpredictably (model, product risk → adversarial and robustness testing). Prioritise by likelihood and impact; discrimination risk is high impact and likely regulated.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Classify each risk by workflow area (development, input data, model) and as project or product risk: (1) the chosen framework contains a known security vulnerability; (2) labels for night images are inconsistent; (3) the model performs much worse on new data than on validation data; (4) the evaluation approach used one small validation split.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Development, project risk. (2) Input data, product risk (poor labels lead to an unreliable model). (3) Model, product risk (overfitting). (4) Development, project risk (poor selection of evaluation approach).

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
ML-specific test levels: input data testing (training data and production data) and ML model testing. Conventional levels by risk: component (UI, data pipeline, communication components), component integration (pipeline-to-model inputs, predictions used by other components, API testing of AIaaS), system (confirmation of ML functional performance once embedded, e.g., after DNN compression; non-functional such as prediction time), system integration (external systems, representative environment), acceptance (suitability of an AI service, ML functional performance criteria).
Risk-based testing: required by most regulatory frameworks. Workflow categorisation: development (project risks: sub-optimal algorithm, poor evaluation approach, framework vulnerabilities), input data (product risks: biased data, pipeline defects, unrepresentative data), model (product risks: missed performance targets, overfitting, adversarial susceptibility). Alternative: ISO/IEC 25059 characteristics. Example mitigations: data pipeline testing, adversarial testing, algorithm/model suitability review.
