lessons.title: 5.1 (part 1) · Input data risks, bias and data pipelines
lessons.summary: Map input data risks to tests, explain how to test for bias, and summarise data pipeline testing at each level.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Input data testing confirms that data used for training, testing and prediction is of sufficient quality. It includes reviews, statistical techniques such as testing for bias, EDA of training data, and static and dynamic testing of the data pipeline. The syllabus maps risks to mitigations. Defects in training data leading to bias, or systemic unfairness from the algorithm, model or framework → testing for bias. Training data from untrustworthy sources, or poorly managed data → data provenance testing. Poisoned training data → A/B testing, data provenance testing, EDA and attacks as part of red teaming. Internally inconsistent datasets, out-of-range data, wrong data types → dataset constraint testing. Sub-optimal feature selection → feature testing. Imbalanced datasets (insufficient coverage of target classes), datasets skewed by augmentation, missing data, data focused on a subset of use cases, or value ranges not covered → data representativeness testing. Poor labelling guidelines, ambiguous data or poor annotation → label correctness testing. Poor pipeline design or integration, data quality defects in pipeline outputs, pipeline performance degradation, security breaches or uncontrolled pipeline changes → data pipeline testing.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A team suspects a competitor added manipulated reviews to a public dataset they scraped. Risk: poisoned training data from an untrustworthy source. Mitigations: data provenance testing (where did each record come from, and was it changed?), EDA to look for anomalous clusters of reviews, an A/B comparison of a model trained with and without the suspicious subset, and red-teaming attacks that try to trigger the poisoned behavior.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Bias in an MLS means non-random, unfair differences in treatment based on sensitive attributes such as gender, age or race; it is not the neuron bias parameter. Bias has two main sources: data bias (unrepresentative data, historical skews, deliberate poisoning) and algorithmic bias (defects in the algorithm, model or framework, such as a decision threshold for credit scores). Dynamic testing with a known unbiased dataset detects bias in outputs whatever its source.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which test addresses 'a categorical field contains integers in some rows and text in others'? Solution: dataset constraint testing (a type constraint). Which addresses 'labelling guidelines for "damaged" are unclear'? Label correctness testing.

blocks.title: Testing for bias and data pipeline testing
blocks.text:
Approaches to detect bias: reviews of the ML workflow, especially data preparation; reviews of dataset documentation (how data was collected and annotated, which populations are represented); static analysis of data preparation and model code for anti-patterns or mishandling of sensitive attributes; EDA with visualisation and clustering to reveal imbalance or anomalous groupings across sensitive attributes; dynamic testing with a known unbiased, representative dataset, looking for statistically significant outcome differences between groups; label correctness testing for mislabelling tied to sensitive attributes; and disparate impact analysis: (1) identify sensitive attributes; (2) generate counterfactuals (for example the same loan application with gender changed); (3) generate model outputs for the counterfactuals; (4) analyse many tests for a statistically significant result showing whether changing the attribute changes the outcome. It can cover combinations of attributes, but counterfactuals must be realistic.

Data pipeline testing uses layers. Design reviews come first. Component testing covers ingestion components, transformation scripts and sensor interfaces with code reviews, static analysis and hardware-specific tests, validates transformation logic and data validation rules, checks error handling, and looks for vulnerabilities that could introduce malware or poisoned data. Component integration testing verifies data flows across internal interfaces and is interpreted correctly. System testing of the assembled pipeline starts with smoke testing, then functional testing (transformations, routing), non-functional testing (load, scalability, security), fault injection with defective data, and back-to-back testing of the operational pipeline against the training pipeline. System integration testing covers data sources, storage, monitoring tools and downstream consumers such as models. Testing in production uses back-to-back testing against previous versions, A/B testing of new pipeline iterations against baselines and real-time monitoring tools. Configuration management reviews check that the correct code versions, configurations and datasets are used in training, testing and production. Training pipelines (often exploratory prototypes) focus on data integrity; operational pipelines prioritise reliability, performance and maintainability.

blocks.title: Worked case: a loan model and counterfactuals
blocks.text: The sensitive attributes are gender and age. The tester takes 2,000 real, anonymised applications, creates counterfactual copies changing only gender, runs both sets through the model and compares approval rates with a statistical test. The difference is significant only for applicants over 60, so the analysis is repeated for the gender-and-age combination. Counterfactuals such as a 19-year-old with 40 years of employment are removed because they are unrealistic.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: For a pipeline that ingests factory sensor readings, transforms units and feeds a predictive-maintenance model, propose one test at each of component, component integration, system, system integration and production level.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Component: unit tests of the unit-conversion script, including validation rules and error handling for malformed readings. Component integration: readings pass from the ingestion service to the transformer with correct field interpretation. System: smoke test, then fault injection with corrupted readings, load tests at peak volume, and back-to-back comparison of the operational pipeline with the training pipeline on the same raw data. System integration: interaction with the sensor gateway, storage and the model as downstream consumer. Production: monitoring, back-to-back with the previous pipeline version, A/B testing of a new iteration against the baseline.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Chapter 5 keywords: data pipeline testing, data representativeness testing, dataset constraint testing, input data testing, label correctness testing, review, testing for bias. AI-specific keywords: disparate impact analysis, multiple annotation.
Risk → mitigation (section 5.1.1): bias → testing for bias; untrustworthy source/poor management → data provenance testing; poisoned data → A/B testing, provenance testing, EDA, red-teaming attacks; inconsistency, out-of-range, wrong types → dataset constraint testing; sub-optimal features → feature testing; imbalance, augmentation skew, missing data, narrow use cases, uncovered ranges → data representativeness testing; poor guidelines, ambiguous data, poor annotation → label correctness testing; pipeline design/integration, data quality, performance degradation, security or uncontrolled changes → data pipeline testing.
Bias sources: data bias, algorithmic bias. Bias tests: workflow reviews, dataset documentation reviews, static analysis, EDA, dynamic testing with unbiased representative data, label correctness testing, disparate impact analysis (4 steps; combinations; realistic counterfactuals).
Pipeline layers: design reviews, component, component integration, system (smoke, functional, non-functional, fault injection, back-to-back with training pipeline), system integration, production (back-to-back, A/B, monitoring), configuration management reviews; training versus operational pipeline priorities.

lessons.title: 5.1 (part 2) · Representativeness, dataset constraints and labels
lessons.summary: Explain representativeness testing, apply dataset constraint testing (K3) and explain label correctness testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Data representativeness testing determines how closely training, validation and test datasets match the real-world data the model will meet in operation. It addresses skewed datasets, missing data, disproportionate feature distributions, inadequate coverage of operational scenarios and imbalanced classes. Steps: (1) define the target population: understand use cases and operational context, analyse users and environments, and identify expected operational distributions and critical edge cases by consulting domain experts, analysing data from existing or similar systems, or using benchmark datasets from trusted sources (such as NIST); then apply stratified sampling to representative reference data to create a baseline covering all relevant subgroups. (2) Analyse data characteristics: apply EDA to the datasets under evaluation and to the reference dataset, visualise distributions with histograms and scatter plots, examine feature relationships and correlations that should be preserved, and identify anomalies, gaps or unusual concentrations. (3) Apply statistical assessment: formal tests such as Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov to compare distributions, checks for class imbalance and verification that typical scenarios and edge or boundary cases are covered. Do this before training, and after deployment monitor operational input data for drift (section 6.1.7).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A speech model will serve callers across a whole country, but 85% of the training audio comes from one region. The reference dataset, built by stratified sampling of real call recordings, shows 30% from that region. EDA histograms of accent, age band and background noise reveal the gap, and a Chi-squared test confirms the regional distribution differs significantly. The team collects more audio from under-represented regions before training.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Representativeness testing compares datasets with the expected operational data; it is not the same as checking each value against a rule (dataset constraint testing) or checking that labels are right (label correctness testing). Kolmogorov-Smirnov appears twice in the syllabus: comparing distributions for representativeness before training, and static drift testing after deployment.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which step comes first: running a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, or defining the target population? Solution: define the target population first; the statistical comparison needs a reference baseline of expected operational data.

blocks.title: Dataset constraint testing and label correctness
blocks.text:
Dataset constraint testing checks whether data satisfies predefined rules, to confirm integrity and consistency. Like a database schema, a set of constraints acts as a logical model the data should satisfy. Single-value constraints apply to one attribute value in one instance: missing (missing values or attributes), range (value within a range) and type (value matches the specified type). Multi-value constraints apply across several instances, typically one attribute across many records: sum (total equals, exceeds or stays below a value, for example total Formula 1 race points cannot exceed 102 and must exceed 50.5), count (number of non-null values), duplicate (identical or near-identical values or instances, limit often zero), useful (an attribute should contain some repeated values; if every value is unique, such as an ID or timestamp, it gives no learnable pattern) and outlier (statistical outliers). Comparison constraints compare different values: greater than (lines of code exceeds lines of code with defects) and correlate (students at least 1.33 standard deviations above the mean mark also have grade A). Checks can be manual, but scale usually requires automating them in the data pipeline, reporting training-data anomalies to data scientists and operational data problems to operations staff.

Label correctness is essential for supervised learning. Approaches: expert review of a sample of labels; multiple annotation, where several annotators label the same data and results are compared back-to-back, with inter-annotator agreement (IAA) measured by Cohen's Kappa or percentage agreement (low IAA points to poor guidelines, ambiguous data or poor annotation); risk-based prioritisation of review and annotation (ambiguous points near class boundaries, data most important for success or safety); data distribution analysis against comparable datasets; automated rule-based tests (bounding boxes must not overlap or extend beyond the image); model loss analysis (high-loss points may be mislabelled); and model confidence score analysis (low-confidence points may be mislabelled, ambiguous or out of distribution). Combining them works best: experts set guidelines early, IAA refines labelling, and model-based checks find remaining defects.

blocks.title: Worked case: constraints for a weather dataset
blocks.text: Attributes: station_id, timestamp, temperature_c, rain_mm, max_temp_c, min_temp_c. Constraints: temperature_c is not missing (single-value, missing); temperature_c between −90 and 60 (single-value, range); rain_mm is a decimal number (type); no duplicate station_id + timestamp pairs (multi-value, duplicate, limit 0); daily rain total per station at most 500 mm (multi-value, sum); max_temp_c ≥ min_temp_c (comparison, greater than); timestamp is unique per row and so not useful as a feature (multi-value, useful). Record 812 has max 12 and min 15: it violates the greater-than constraint and is reported to the data scientists.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A patient dataset has attributes: patient_id, age, sex, systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, diagnosis. Write five constraints, each labelled single-value, multi-value or comparison, and give one record that violates each.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) age is present (single-value, missing): a record with empty age violates it. (2) age between 0 and 120 (single-value, range): age 154. (3) sex is one of the specified category codes (single-value, type): sex = 3.7. (4) no two records with the same patient_id (multi-value, duplicate): two rows with id 1042. (5) systolic_bp greater than diastolic_bp (comparison, greater than): 80/120. A further multi-value example is a count constraint: at least 1,000 non-null diagnosis values.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-5.1.7)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. For a structured tabular dataset, write automated checks for missing values, duplicate rows and outliers (for example values more than three standard deviations from the mean), run them, and summarise the findings in a short report addressed to the data scientists.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Representativeness steps: define target population (use cases, context, users, environments; expected distributions and edge cases via domain experts, existing or similar systems, trusted benchmark datasets such as NIST; stratified sampling of reference data as baseline); analyse data characteristics (EDA of datasets and reference, histograms, scatter plots, correlations, anomalies, gaps); statistical assessment (Chi-squared, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, class imbalance, typical and edge/boundary cases). Before training; monitor for drift after deployment.
Dataset constraints: single-value (missing, range, type); multi-value (sum, count, duplicate, useful, outlier); comparison (greater than, correlate). Automate in the pipeline; reports to data scientists (training anomalies) or operations staff (operational problems).
Label correctness: expert review, multiple annotation (back-to-back; IAA by Cohen's Kappa or percentage agreement), risk-based prioritisation, data distribution analysis, automated rule-based tests (bounding boxes), model loss analysis, model confidence score analysis; combine approaches.

lessons.title: 6.1 (part 1) · Model risks, documentation, statistics, adversarial and metamorphic testing
lessons.summary: Map model risks to tests, review model documentation, test probabilistic performance statistically, explain adversarial testing and use metamorphic testing (K3).

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: ML model testing addresses functional risks (bias, overfitting, adversarial vulnerability), non-functional risks (lack of AI robustness, performance efficiency) and deployment risks. Risk-to-mitigation examples from the syllabus: biased or unfair model → testing for bias; unethical model → ethical system testing; adversarial examples → adversarial testing; overfitted or underfitted model → testing for overfitting or underfitting; unacceptable data or concept drift → drift testing; side-effects → side-effects testing; reward hacking → reward hacking testing; model API defect → API testing; failure to achieve required performance measures → ML functional performance testing; functional incorrectness and non-functional defects → metamorphic testing; test oracle problem → metamorphic, back-to-back and A/B testing; poor system requirements → requirements review, red teaming and exploratory testing; lack of robustness to unexpected inputs → adversarial testing and fuzz testing; inadequate performance efficiency → performance testing; poor model documentation → model documentation review; model updates that introduce defects → back-to-back testing; model updates that decrease performance → A/B testing; immediate failure of an updated deployment → smoke testing; regression after deployment → regression testing; security, safety, privacy violations and harmful outputs → red teaming.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A recommendation model's new version is ready. Risk: the update decreases ML functional performance → A/B testing against the current version on agreed metrics. Risk: the update introduces defects in specific cases → back-to-back testing against the current version. Risk: deployment fails immediately → smoke testing. Risk: the model learns to exploit its reward (for example recommending clickbait) → reward hacking testing.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Metamorphic testing does not need the expected output of each test case; it needs a metamorphic relation describing how a change to the inputs should change (or not change) the outputs. It usually starts from a source test case that passed. It finds relational flaws, not every absolute error, so combine it with other techniques. Incorrect or incomplete relations give false confidence.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A requirement says '98% accuracy with a margin of error of ±4% at a 95% confidence level'. If you keep the confidence level fixed and run more tests, what happens? Solution: the margin of error decreases, so the result becomes more precise. If you keep the margin of error fixed, the confidence level increases, so the result becomes more certain.

blocks.title: Documentation, statistics and adversarial testing
blocks.text:
Model documentation is critical because machine-generated models are hard to understand, black-box in nature, data-dependent and frequently updated. Transparency lets stakeholders trace behavior, decision logic and data lineage, and regulation such as the EU AI Act requires clear documentation; for high-risk systems a documentation audit is often a prerequisite for deployment. Frameworks include Model Cards (intended uses, evaluation results, ethical considerations) and Datasheets for Datasets (motivation, composition, collection process, uses). Checklist areas: general (identifiers, version, developer, licence, hardware), design (assumptions, technical decisions, algorithm), usage (intended purpose, users, self-learning approach, bias, ethics, safety, transparency, thresholds, platform, drift), datasets (features, source, collection, preprocessing, labels, size, privacy, security, fairness, restrictions), testing (test dataset details, independence, results, activities), functional (measures, validation dataset, thresholds, actual performance), non-functional (scalability, reliability, availability, performance efficiency, maintainability, robustness) and operational (deployment plan and environment, resources, monitoring metrics and alerts, retraining strategy, update/rollback and deprecation plans, security, explainability methods). Reviews aim to find missing, inaccurate or inconsistent information, improve clarity and maintainability, give enough information for test and deployment, and verify regulatory requirements.

ML functional performance testing of probabilistic systems moves beyond a single pass/fail to statistically measuring performance against acceptance criteria expressed with a metric, a margin of error (MoE) and a confidence level (CL); these determine the minimum number of tests. In the syllabus example, '98% accuracy, MoE ±4% at 95% CL' needs 601 test cases, of which at least 589 must pass; with observed 98% accuracy the actual MoE is about ±1.1%, and sequential testing can stop early (about 170 tests if accuracy stays at or above 98%). A safety requirement of '99% reliability with 95% confidence' needs 299 tests that all pass. You are not asked to compute these values in the exam. The test dataset must be large, independent of training and validation data, and representative of the operational input domain; results are reported with statistical confidence, for example 'accuracy 94% ±4% at 95% CL'.

Adversarial testing feeds slightly perturbed inputs, often imperceptible to humans, to make the model mispredict; successful ones are adversarial examples, whether met accidentally or used maliciously in adversarial attacks. Black-box approaches build an equivalent model with known internals, create adversarial inputs from it and rely on transferability (equivalent models share classification boundaries), or use brute force with very many tests. White-box approaches use knowledge of the architecture, parameters and training process. It can be manual or automated, and the attack landscape evolves constantly.

blocks.title: Worked case: metamorphic testing of a house-price model
blocks.text: No affordable oracle says what the exact price of a house should be. A source test case: a 120 m² house with 3 bedrooms in district D is predicted at 410,000, judged plausible. Metamorphic relations: MR1 (monotonicity) adding 20 m² of living area, other inputs unchanged, should not decrease the prediction; MR2 (invariance) changing the listing ID or the order of input fields should not change the prediction; MR3 (consistency) predicting the same house twice in one session gives the same value. Follow-up test cases: the same house at 140 m² (expect ≥ 410,000); the same house with a new listing ID (expect 410,000). If the 140 m² prediction is 395,000, MR1 is violated and a defect is reported.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A risk-assessment model predicts age at death from lifestyle data. Derive two metamorphic relations, one where the follow-up output should change in a known direction and one where it should stay the same, then write one follow-up test case for each from the source case 'non-smoker, 45, BMI 24, predicted 84'.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: MR1 (monotonicity): increasing the number of cigarettes smoked per day, other inputs unchanged, should decrease (not increase) the prediction. Follow-up: the same person smoking 20 cigarettes a day; expect a prediction below 84. MR2 (invariance): changing an irrelevant identifier such as the record number should leave the prediction unchanged. Follow-up: the same data with a different record number; expect 84. Both follow-ups check relations between outputs, not exact expected values. Validate the relations with domain experts, because an incorrect relation gives false confidence.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-6.1.6)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. For a model you can call (for example a sentiment classifier), derive several MRs, some where source and follow-up results should be the same and some where they should differ; generate source test cases, derive and run follow-ups, and note which relations fail. Remember the limitation when source test cases are not known to pass.

blocks.text:
Chapter 6 keywords: A/B testing, adversarial testing, back-to-back testing, concept drift, data drift, drift testing, metamorphic testing, ML functional performance, ML model testing, review. AI-specific keywords: overfitting, underfitting.
Model risk table (section 6.1.1): see the Understand block; note ethical system testing, side-effects testing, reward hacking testing, fuzz testing, smoke and regression testing after deployment, and red teaming for security, safety, privacy and harmful outputs.
Documentation: Model Cards, Datasheets for Datasets; checklist areas general, design, usage, datasets, testing, functional, non-functional, operational; review aims (missing/inaccurate/inconsistent information, clarity, maintainability, enough information for test and deployment, regulatory requirements).
Statistical performance testing: metric + MoE + CL; fix CL → MoE shrinks (more precise); fix MoE → CL rises (more certain); independent, representative test data; report with confidence; sequential testing for early stopping; formulae not examined.
Adversarial testing: perturbations, adversarial examples and attacks; black box (equivalent model and transferability, brute force), white box; manual or automated.
Metamorphic testing: source test case (usually passed) → follow-up test cases via a metamorphic relation based on a required property; objectives consistency, monotonicity, invariance; chosen when no reliable expected outputs, black box, or relational properties suffice; MRs from domain knowledge, requirements or domain properties (laws of physics); validate MRs by expert review, reference models and edge-case coverage; limits: incorrect/incomplete MRs, relational not absolute errors.

lessons.title: 6.1 (part 2) · Drift, fitting, A/B and back-to-back testing
lessons.summary: Explain drift testing, detect overfitting and underfitting, and use A/B and back-to-back testing for ML systems.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Drift testing identifies two forms of drift in operational models. Data drift: the statistical properties of operational input data change over time, for example a spam filter meeting new phishing styles that did not exist during training, or seasonal behavior. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the correct output changes, for example new financial regulations reclassify a 'low-risk' transaction type as 'high-risk', so the model's learned decision boundary becomes outdated and accuracy falls. Dynamic drift testing needs current ground truth from user feedback, direct (a user rates a film recommendation) or indirect (which films the user actually watched); the difference between ground truth and model output is compared with a threshold. Static drift testing does not need ground truth: it compares the statistical properties of input and predicted-output distributions using a test such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov; a significant difference indicates drift.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A grocery demand model receives no immediate ground truth because actual sales arrive weeks later. Each week the team compares the distribution of incoming features and predictions with the training-period distributions using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (static drift testing). When actual sales arrive, they compare them with predictions and alert when the error exceeds 8% (dynamic drift testing).

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Data drift changes the inputs; concept drift changes what the right answer is for the same inputs. Static drift testing needs no ground truth; dynamic drift testing does. Overfitting shows up as much worse performance on new data than during evaluation; underfitting shows as low performance on both training and validation data.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Training accuracy 99%, validation accuracy 97%, test accuracy 78% on data including rarer examples. What does this suggest? Solution: likely overfitting, because the model performs significantly worse on the independent test dataset than on the validation dataset. If training and validation accuracy were both around 60% and close together, underfitting would be suspected.

blocks.title: Fitting, A/B testing and back-to-back testing
blocks.text:
Overfitting, underfitting and right-fitting are the three possible outcomes, and testing for the first two belongs in training, evaluation and tuning. An overfitted model learns the training data too well, capturing noise rather than the underlying pattern, and generalises poorly. Test by evaluating it on a separate test dataset not used in training that includes some less common examples; significantly worse results than on validation data suggest overfitting. An underfitted model is too simple, or the training data lacks features that reflect important input-output relationships; metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall or F1 are consistently low on both training and validation sets, and learning curves show training and validation errors staying high and close together without much improvement.

A/B testing compares the responses of two variants, A and B, to the same inputs to decide which is better. It is statistical and usually needs multiple test runs; popular techniques are the t-test, z-test, chi-squared test and Mann-Whitney U test. It addresses the test oracle problem by using the existing system as a partial oracle, but it does not generate test cases or guide test design, although operational inputs are often used. With agreed acceptance criteria, such as ML functional performance metrics, it shows that an updated variant performs as well as or better than the previous one; examples range from a simple classifier to a smart-city routing system compared on average commute times over consecutive weeks. Self-learning systems can use it automatically: after each change, run tests and compare; keep the change if better, otherwise revert.

Back-to-back testing uses an alternative version of the system as a pseudo-oracle and compares its outputs with the system under test for the same inputs. The pseudo-oracle may be an existing system or one built for testing (at a cost), ideally by an independent team using different frameworks, algorithms or settings, because shared components (common with reused open-source AI components) could make both produce the same wrong output. Conventional software can serve as a pseudo-oracle if it solves the same problem. For functional back-to-back testing, the pseudo-oracle only needs matching functional behavior, not the same non-functional qualities, which can make it cheaper. Only test inputs are needed, not expected results; inputs can come from existing tests such as regression suites or be generated from training data. It is valuable when migrating an MLS between environments (development to production) and reveals subtle defects in edge cases. The key difference: A/B testing compares two variants with performance metrics and statistics; back-to-back testing detects defects.

blocks.title: Worked case: migrating a model to production
blocks.text: A credit model moves from a data-science notebook to a production service with a different serving library. The team sends 50,000 historical applications to both versions and flags every case where the decisions differ (back-to-back testing): 37 differences reveal a rounding defect in the production feature scaler. After fixing it, they run the new production model as variant B against the current production model A on live traffic for two weeks and compare approval accuracy with a chi-squared test (A/B testing).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose drift, overfitting/underfitting, A/B or back-to-back testing for each situation: (1) a retrained fraud model must perform at least as well as the current one on agreed metrics; (2) an independently developed rule-based system is available that solves the same classification problem; (3) training and validation error both stay high across epochs; (4) a translation model's predicted-output distribution changes sharply after a product launch.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) A/B testing with the agreed metrics and a statistical test. (2) Back-to-back testing with the rule-based system as pseudo-oracle (it only needs matching functional behavior). (3) Testing for underfitting (learning curves and consistently low metrics). (4) Static drift testing (distribution comparison such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov); confirm with ground truth when it becomes available.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Drift: data drift (input statistics change: new phishing types, seasonality, behavior shifts) and concept drift (input-output relationship changes: new regulation reclassifies transactions). Dynamic drift testing: needs current ground truth from direct or indirect user feedback, difference vs threshold. Static drift testing: compares input and predicted-output distributions (Kolmogorov-Smirnov), no ground truth needed.
Overfitting: memorises noise, poor generalisation; test on separate test data including less common examples; much worse than validation. Underfitting: too simple or missing features; low metrics on training and validation; learning curves high and close. Test during training, evaluation and tuning.
A/B testing: two variants, same inputs, statistical (t-test, z-test, chi-squared, Mann-Whitney U), existing system as partial oracle, no test generation, needs agreed acceptance criteria, also for self-learning systems (accept or revert).
Back-to-back testing: pseudo-oracle (existing or purpose-built; independent team, different frameworks, algorithms or settings; conventional software possible), avoid shared components; functional match only; inputs only, no expected results (from regression suites or generated from training data); useful when migrating environments and for edge cases. A/B compares variants with metrics; back-to-back detects defects.

lessons.title: 7.1 · ML development testing and deployment testing
lessons.summary: Map ML development risks to tests and explain installability, rollback, canary, shadow, model conversion, cross-device and API testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: ML development testing addresses risks introduced by development tools, configuration choices and deployment mechanisms rather than by the model itself. Risk-to-mitigation examples: incorrect or unintended use of library or framework APIs (TensorFlow, PyTorch) → API testing; sub-optimal framework selection → framework suitability review; systemic unfairness from algorithm, model or framework → testing for bias; defective framework installation or build → smoke testing; defective implementation of evaluation by the framework → reviews of framework evaluation code and cross-checking evaluation results (for example against manual benchmarks); poor framework performance efficiency → performance testing; poor framework usability → usability testing; a defect in a library used by the framework, or a defective algorithm implementation → ML functional performance testing and back-to-back testing; framework security vulnerabilities → security testing; poor framework documentation → framework documentation review; sub-optimal algorithm selection → algorithm suitability review and A/B testing; sub-optimal hyperparameters (network structure, learning rate) → ML functional performance testing and A/B testing; defective allocation of data to training, validation and test sets → data allocation review; poor choice of evaluation approach (such as k-fold cross-validation) → ML functional performance testing; misinterpreting results because learning is stochastic → ML functional performance testing; deployment defects from generating a platform-specific version → smoke, ML functional performance and A/B testing; a deployed model incompatible with its environment → smoke testing and MLS deployment testing; a deployed model that is no improvement over the current one → shadow testing.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: After upgrading the ML framework, the team's evaluation script reports 3% higher F1 than before with the same model. Risk: defective evaluation implementation by the framework. Mitigation: review the framework's evaluation code path and cross-check the metric by calculating F1 manually from the confusion matrix on a sample.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Shadow testing does not affect live responses: the new model receives the same live requests as the production model, but only the production model's answers are returned. Canary testing does affect real users: a small share of traffic (for example 5%) is actually served by the new model. Rollback testing is done before deployment to confirm rollback readiness, not only after a failure.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which deployment test fits 'compare the new model with the current one on live data without any risk to users'? Solution: shadow testing. Which fits 'release to 5% of users and watch latency, accuracy and error rates before full rollout'? Canary testing.

blocks.title: Deployment testing
blocks.text: Deploying an MLS to its target environment (cloud, edge device, mobile) involves several test types. Installability testing: install, configure and uninstall across all supported environments, including dependencies such as GPU drivers, framework compatibility and installation scripts. Rollback testing: the system can revert to a previously stable state after a degraded or failed deployment, covering only the model or the whole system including the data pipeline; it must be done before deployment. Canary testing: release the updated model to a small subset of production traffic and monitor real-time metrics such as latency, accuracy and error rates to catch regressions before full rollout. Shadow testing: run the new model in parallel with the production model on the same live requests without affecting live responses, comparing them on live data at low risk and revealing performance regressions or data drift. Model conversion testing: after converting from the training format to a deployment format, the model keeps acceptable predictive accuracy, consistent behavior and operational efficiency (inference speed, memory). Cross-device testing: correct performance across the intended targets from mobile and edge devices to cloud servers. API testing: well-defined, standards-compliant interfaces; correct handling of inputs and outputs, error messages, and integration with data feeds, clients and the pipeline.

blocks.title: Worked case: a model for phones and the cloud
blocks.text: A vision model trained in a framework's native format is converted to a mobile format and also served from the cloud. Tests: model conversion testing compares accuracy, inference time and memory of the converted model with the original on the same test set; cross-device testing runs it on low-end and high-end phones and on the cloud server; installability testing checks the app installs with the right runtime libraries; rollback testing confirms before release that the previous model can be restored; shadow testing runs the new cloud model alongside the current one for a week; canary testing then releases it to 5% of users.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Name the deployment test for each risk: (1) after quantization for an edge chip, predictions differ from the original model; (2) the release cannot be undone if the pipeline fails; (3) the model works on the developer's GPU but the installation script fails on servers without a specific driver; (4) the new model's error messages break a client application.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Model conversion testing (accuracy, consistent behavior and efficiency after conversion). (2) Rollback testing, performed before deployment, possibly covering the data pipeline. (3) Installability testing (dependencies such as GPU drivers, installation scripts). (4) API testing (error messages and integration with clients).

blocks.text:
Chapter 7 keywords: ML development testing, ML functional performance, shadow testing.
Development risks and mitigations: framework/library API misuse → API testing; framework selection → framework suitability review; systemic unfairness → testing for bias; installation/build → smoke testing; evaluation implementation → review evaluation code, cross-check results; framework performance → performance testing; usability → usability testing; library defect or defective algorithm implementation → ML functional performance testing, back-to-back testing; framework security → security testing; framework documentation → documentation review; algorithm selection → algorithm suitability review, A/B testing; hyperparameters → ML functional performance testing, A/B testing; data allocation → data allocation review; evaluation approach and stochastic interpretation → ML functional performance testing; deployment defect → smoke, ML functional performance, A/B testing; incompatible environment → smoke testing, MLS deployment testing; no improvement → shadow testing.
Deployment tests: installability, rollback (before deployment; model or whole system), canary (small subset of traffic, e.g., 5%; latency, accuracy, error rates), shadow (parallel, same live requests, no effect on live responses), model conversion (accuracy, consistency, inference speed, memory), cross-device (mobile, edge, cloud), API (standards-compliant interfaces, inputs/outputs, error messages, integration).

lessons.title: Final revision · Turn evidence into an exam decision
lessons.summary: Review key distinctions, the four K3 skills and timed-exam strategy for CT-AI v2.0.

blocks.title: Recall and distinguish
blocks.text: Explain each pair with an example: conventional versus AI-based system; narrow versus general versus super AI; development versus hosting; user controllability versus intervenability; transparency versus explainability; classification versus ML regression; clustering versus association; model versus algorithm hyperparameters; evaluation versus testing; fine-tuning versus RAG; validation versus test dataset; precision versus recall; neuron coverage versus kMNC versus NBC; locked versus adaptive; red teaming versus blue teaming versus benchmarking; input data testing versus model testing; data bias versus algorithmic bias; data drift versus concept drift; static versus dynamic drift testing; overfitting versus underfitting; A/B versus back-to-back testing; shadow versus canary testing.

blocks.title: K3 checklist
blocks.text: AI-3.3.1: read the matrix orientation, write TP, FP, FN, TN, then accuracy (all correct / all), precision (TP / predicted positive), recall (TP / actual positive), F1 (2PR / (P + R)). AI-4.2.2: diverse team → safe environment → prompting (exploration or checklists, multi-turn) → analyse failures → datasets for mitigation; distinguish security from safety red teaming. AI-5.1.5: classify each rule as single-value (missing, range, type), multi-value (sum, count, duplicate, useful, outlier) or comparison (greater than, correlate), then find the violating record. AI-6.1.5: start from a passed source test case, state the property, derive the relation (same, increase, decrease), build the follow-up case and say what result would reveal a failure.

blocks.title: Timed strategy
blocks.text: Forty questions in 60 minutes leaves 1.5 minutes per question on average; the four K3 items deserve about three minutes each. Read each stem for BEST, MOST LIKELY, LEAST and NOT, and for the required selection count. Calculate on scratch paper and check the denominator before choosing. Unanswered questions score zero, so answer everything. Answers and explanations appear after submitting the mock or when its timer expires.

blocks.title: Review after a paper
blocks.text: For each mistake, name the objective, explain why your option failed and why the key fits better, re-read the linked lesson section and write a new example of your own. Treat correct guesses as mistakes for review. Use short sessions to practise weak chapters, remembering that practice can expose questions from unopened papers. A repeated paper is useful revision, but it cannot provide fresh readiness evidence.

blocks.title: Explain a full test strategy
blocks.text: Pick an AI-based product you know, for example a loan-approval system. Explain its quality characteristics and acceptance criteria; how it was built (forms of ML, workflow, data preparation, datasets); its oracle problem and how you would test it statistically; its risks by workflow area; and the input data, model, development and deployment tests you would run. If you cannot link two decisions, revisit the relevant lesson.

blocks.title: Map risks to tests quickly
blocks.text: Data: bias → testing for bias; provenance → data provenance testing; rules → dataset constraint testing; coverage → representativeness testing; labels → label correctness testing; pipeline → data pipeline testing. Model: performance → ML functional performance testing; perturbations → adversarial testing; oracle → metamorphic, back-to-back, A/B; drift → drift testing; fitting → overfitting/underfitting tests; harmful outputs → red teaming. Development: frameworks → suitability and documentation reviews, API, smoke, security, performance and usability testing; deployment → installability, rollback, canary, shadow, model conversion, cross-device and API testing.

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes a key difference between conventional systems and AI-based systems that use machine learning?

options.text: Conventional systems learn from labelled examples, while ML-based systems follow step-by-step rules written by developers
Conventional systems are probabilistic and hard to explain, while ML-based systems are deterministic and transparent
Conventional systems adapt continuously after release, while ML-based systems change only through manual updates
Conventional systems follow explicitly programmed instructions, while ML-based systems derive their behavior from patterns learned from data

questions.explanation: Conventional systems are programmed imperatively with explicit instructions, so their behavior is predictable; most ML-based systems learn patterns from data instead. The other options reverse the characteristics: AI-based systems tend to be probabilistic, less explainable and possibly self-learning. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); AI-1.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes narrow AI from general AI?

options.text: Narrow AI describes AI that runs offline, while general AI describes AI that has access to the internet during operation
Narrow AI improves itself without human control, while general AI needs human retraining for each new task it performs
Narrow AI is limited to rule-based expert systems, while general AI covers every machine learning system deployed today
Narrow AI performs specific tasks in a limited domain, while general AI would handle most intellectual tasks a human can without retraining

questions.explanation: Narrow (weak) AI is designed for specific tasks and represents all deployed AI today; general (strong) AI would learn and apply knowledge across a broad range of tasks without retraining. Self-improvement without control describes super AI, and internet access is not the distinguishing factor. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.2 (p. 15); AI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO pairings of an AI technology with a typical use are correct? Select TWO.

options.text: Expert systems: discovering clusters in unlabelled customer purchase data
Fuzzy logic: generating realistic synthetic images from random noise
Convolutional neural networks: object detection in camera images
Search algorithms: learning class labels from a large labelled image dataset
Recurrent neural networks: processing sequential data such as sensor time series

questions.explanation: CNNs are effective for image recognition and object detection, and RNNs specialise in sequential data such as text or time series. Fuzzy logic reasons under uncertainty, search algorithms solve optimisation problems, and expert systems apply explicit rules; image generation, supervised labelling and clustering belong to other technologies. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); AI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST explains generative AI?

options.text: It is limited to producing text, because image and audio generation require rule-based systems instead of learned models
It improves existing content by compressing it, which is why it is used mainly for reducing the size of training datasets
It creates new content such as text, images or audio that resembles the data it learned from, and many such systems can also classify and predict
It analyses existing content to assign labels and extract insights, but it cannot produce content that did not exist before

questions.explanation: GenAI specialises in creating new content that resembles its training data, and many GenAI systems also support classification and prediction. Labelling without generation describes discriminative models, compression is not its purpose, and GenAI covers images, video, music and audio as well as text. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.4 (p. 17); AI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why do GPUs typically outperform CPUs for training ML models?

options.text: GPUs support more complex high-precision operations than CPUs, which ML training depends on
GPUs run at higher clock speeds than CPUs, which shortens each sequential step of the model's training loop
GPUs avoid the von Neumann architecture, which removes the memory bottleneck of neural networks
GPUs provide thousands of simple cores for massively parallel computation such as matrix multiplication

questions.explanation: GPUs have thousands of cores designed for massively parallel, relatively simple processing, which suits ML. CPUs usually have higher clock speeds and high-precision support that ML rarely needs, and avoiding the von Neumann architecture describes neuromorphic processors. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.5 (p. 18); AI-1.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST compares acquiring a third-party AI service with developing a private AI-based system?

options.text: A third-party service removes the need for acceptance testing, while a private system removes the need for API testing
A private system can be deployed faster, while a third-party service needs specialised in-house data scientists
A third-party pretrained model or AIaaS can shorten time to market, while a private system can be tailored but needs specialised skills
A third-party AIaaS gives full control over training data, while a private system depends on the vendor's update schedule

questions.explanation: Third-party systems typically come as pretrained models or AI as a Service, enabling faster deployment and quicker time to market; private systems can be better tailored but require specialised skills in-house or outsourced. Acceptance and API testing remain relevant when AI is used as a service. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.6 (p. 18); AI-1.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A navigation app updates its route suggestions on its own after a new motorway opens, without being redeployed. Which ISO/IEC 25059 characteristic does this behavior demonstrate?

options.text: User controllability
Functional adaptability
Intervenability
AI functional correctness

questions.explanation: Functional adaptability is the ability of an AI-based system to adapt autonomously to changes in its operational environment after deployment. User controllability and intervenability concern humans intervening, and AI functional correctness concerns acceptable rates of correct and incorrect outputs. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.1 (p. 22); AI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes a key challenge when AI is used in a safety-related system?

options.text: Self-learning can move the system's behavior away from the behavior that was tested before deployment, undermining the safety argument
Mature functional safety standards require the latest deep learning techniques, which slows the release of new systems
Self-learning systems stop adapting after deployment, so safety depends on frequent manual updates by operators
Detailed safety requirements leave the model too little room to learn the implicit goals contained in its training data

questions.explanation: Rigorous pre-deployment testing demonstrates safety integrity, but a self-learning system progressively moves away from its tested behavior. Requirements for AI often start vague rather than too detailed, self-learning systems keep adapting, and mature safety standards often exclude or even prohibit AI. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.2 (p. 23); AI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which example is LEAST likely to be a valid acceptance criterion for an AI-specific quality characteristic defined in ISO/IEC 25059?

options.text: A patrol robot stops all motion within 0.5 seconds after a guard triggers an all-stop command to prevent a collision
A greenhouse controller adapts its watering plan within 20 minutes when humidity deviates by more than 10% from optimum
When a scan is flagged as high risk, the tool displays which image regions most influenced the result
The spam filter settings page is easy to understand and requires minimal technical expertise to maintain

questions.explanation: Ease of understanding and maintenance is a general usability or maintainability concern and is not measurable as written. The other options are measurable criteria for intervenability, functional adaptability and transparency of AI-based systems. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); AI-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Given these forms of ML:
1. Clustering
2. Reinforcement learning
3. Classification
4. ML regression
And these examples:
A. A smart thermostat adjusts its heating schedule after receiving rewards for comfort and energy savings
B. A dealer estimates the selling price of a used car from its age, mileage and condition
C. A news site groups unlabelled articles by topic
D. A payment service decides whether a transaction is fraudulent using a labelled history
Which matching is BEST?
questions.explanation: Grouping unlabelled articles is clustering; learning from rewards is reinforcement learning; deciding fraud or not from labelled data is classification; estimating a continuous price is ML regression. Each distractor swaps at least two of these pairs. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.1 (p. 27); AI-3.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Given these ML workflow activities:
1. Evaluate the model
2. Test the model
3. Deploy the model
4. Prepare & test data
And these descriptions:
A. An independent dataset is used to verify that the agreed ML functional performance criteria are met
B. Candidate models are compared using metrics measured on the validation dataset
C. The model is re-engineered with its data pipeline for the target platform and checked again
D. The provenance of the data and the automated preprocessing steps are checked
Which matching is BEST?
questions.explanation: Evaluation uses the validation dataset to compare and improve models; testing uses an independent test dataset against the agreed criteria; deployment re-engineers the model with its pipeline and retests it; data preparation includes testing the data and automated preparation steps. The distractors swap evaluation with testing or deployment with data preparation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.2 (p. 28); AI-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is correct?

options.text: Additional layers containing task-specific documents are added to the neural network and then trained, which changes the original pretrained model
Relevant documents from task-specific data sources are retrieved and added to an enhanced prompt, and the pretrained model is not changed
Task-specific documents replace the pretrained model, so the system answers prompts by keyword retrieval without an LLM
The pretrained model is retrained on all task-specific documents, so its weights are adjusted before each prompt is answered

questions.explanation: RAG transforms task-specific data sources into a searchable format, retrieves documents relevant to the prompt and includes them in an enhanced prompt passed to the LLM; no change is made to the pretrained model. Adding or retraining layers describes fine-tuning, and RAG still uses the LLM. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.4 (p. 30); AI-3.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which activity is part of data preprocessing?

options.text: Selecting the features that contribute most to the model's ML performance
Imputing missing values in a numeric column using the median of that column
Plotting histograms to discover trends and anomalies in the collected data
Identifying whether the required data is numerical, categorical, image or text

questions.explanation: Cleaning, including imputing missing values with the mean, median or mode, is data preprocessing. Identifying data types belongs to data acquisition, selecting features is feature engineering, and plotting to discover patterns is exploratory data analysis. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.2.1 (p. 31); AI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST contrasts the roles of the training, validation and test datasets?

options.text: The training dataset and test dataset are identical, and the validation dataset contains only edge cases rejected during training
The training dataset tests the tuned model, the validation dataset fits the model, and the test dataset guides the hyperparameter tuning
The training dataset fits the model, the validation dataset evaluates it to guide tuning, and the test dataset checks the tuned model
The training dataset guides tuning, the validation dataset checks the deployed model, and the test dataset fits the model weights

questions.explanation: The training dataset is used to train the model, the validation dataset to evaluate and then tune it, and the test (holdout) dataset to test the tuned model. The three should be equivalent, for example randomly selected from one representative dataset. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.2.3 (p. 32); AI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt:
A defect-prediction model is tested on 200 modules. The confusion matrix gives these counts:
Predicted defective: actual defective 72, actual clean 18
Predicted clean: actual defective 8, actual clean 102
What is the recall of the model?
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 72 / (72 + 8) = 90.0%. 80.0% is precision, 72 / (72 + 18); 87.0% is accuracy, (72 + 102) / 200; and 84.7% is the F1-score of these precision and recall values. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.3.1 (p. 33); AI-3.3.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: How is the activation value of a neuron in a hidden layer of a deep neural network calculated?

options.text: The input pixel values are passed unchanged to the neuron, which outputs the largest weight among its connections
The neuron's bias is multiplied by the number of its incoming connections, and the result is compared with the expected output
The activation values of the next layer are averaged and copied back into the neuron during each forward pass
The weighted sum of the previous layer's activation values plus the neuron's bias is passed through an activation function

questions.explanation: Each neuron computes a weighted sum of the activation values of connected neurons in the previous layer, adds its own bias and passes the result through a non-linear activation function. The other options misdescribe the computation or the direction of information flow. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.4.1 (p. 36); AI-3.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST compares the testability of locked and adaptive AI-based systems?

options.text: Locked systems are easier to test because they are largely deterministic, while adaptive systems may change their behavior during or because of testing
Adaptive systems are easier to test because expected results stay fixed, while locked systems change after deployment
Adaptive systems are easier to test because they correct their own defects, while locked systems need retraining before each test cycle
Locked and adaptive systems are equally testable, because both are deterministic once their training data has been frozen

questions.explanation: Locked systems keep fixed behavior after deployment, so expected results do not change; adaptive systems can change during or as a result of testing, and their new behaviors cannot be predicted in advance. Adaptive systems do not correct their own defects, and it is locked systems whose expected results stay fixed. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.1 (p. 39); AI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An image classifier labels one photo of a cat as a dog. Why is this single result NOT enough to judge the model's AI functional correctness?

options.text: The model behaves probabilistically, so a statistically significant number of tests is needed to assess its overall correctness
The model behaves adaptively, so the result must be repeated on the training data before it is reported
The model behaves deterministically, so the single failure proves the model is wrong for all cat images
The model behaves randomly, so neither one test nor many tests can say anything about its correctness

questions.explanation: AI-based systems are probabilistic and often non-deterministic, so a single test cannot accurately reflect overall AI functional correctness; the test suite must be large enough for statistically significant results. The behavior is neither purely deterministic nor entirely random, and retesting on training data would not show generalisation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.2 (p. 40); AI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which test oracle difficulty is caused by self-learning AI-based systems?

options.text: The system's correct behavior changes over time, so an initial set of expected results can quickly become invalid
The system's requirements are complete and detailed, so testers have too many expected results to check
The system's outputs never vary, so testers cannot observe the behavior they need in order to define expected results
The system's outputs are too complex for human experts, so expected results must be calculated by hand

questions.explanation: Self-learning systems update their internal models with new data after deployment, so the definition of 'correct' evolves and earlier expected results can quickly become invalid. Task complexity is a separate difficulty, AI requirements are often incomplete, and AI outputs can vary. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.3 (p. 40); AI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the 'input explosion problem' when testing a GenAI system?

options.text: Inputs are highly diverse and hard to control: system and user prompts, API access, parameters such as temperature, and the context window all affect output
Test inputs must be generated faster than the model can respond, so automated tools overload the API during black-box testing
The number of model parameters grows with each prompt, so the system eventually runs out of memory and stops responding
Each prompt is stored permanently in the training data, so the model's size increases with every test case that testers execute

questions.explanation: The input explosion problem arises because GenAI inputs can be highly diverse: optional system prompts, user prompts with large amounts of data, API access, parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and the context window. The other options describe mechanisms that are not part of the syllabus explanation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.1 (p. 41); AI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
You lead red teaming for a GenAI medical-information chatbot before release. Given these steps:
i. Analyse the identified failures to understand the threats
ii. Give the testers access to the chatbot in a safe test environment
iii. Assemble a team covering a wide range of perspectives and attack vectors
iv. Create datasets from the threats to support mitigations and improvements
v. Prompt the chatbot, through open-ended exploration or checklists, to find vulnerabilities
In which order should the steps be performed?

options.text: iii, v, ii, i, iv
ii, iii, v, iv, i
iii, ii, v, i, iv
v, i, iii, ii, iv

questions.explanation: Red teaming assembles a diverse team first, provides access in a safe environment, prompts the system to identify vulnerabilities, analyses the failures to understand threats, and finally creates datasets from the threats to support mitigations. Analysis must precede dataset creation, and the team needs access before prompting. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.2 (p. 42); AI-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which two test levels are specific to machine learning systems according to the CT-AI syllabus?

options.text: Input data testing and ML model testing
Training testing and deployment testing
Neuron testing and layer testing
Prompt testing and output testing

questions.explanation: The two specialised test levels that address ML-specific risks are input data testing (training and production data) and ML model testing. The other pairs are not test levels defined in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.1 (p. 43); AI-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Using the ML workflow to categorise risks, which is an example of a project risk in the development area?

options.text: A data pipeline that corrupts sensor readings
A model that is susceptible to adversarial examples
Training data that is biased against older users
Selecting a sub-optimal algorithm for the problem

questions.explanation: Development risks concern the algorithm, model development and framework; examples are sub-optimal algorithm selection, poor selection of evaluation approach and framework security vulnerabilities. Biased data and pipeline defects are input data risks, and adversarial susceptibility is a model risk. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.2 (p. 44); AI-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO input data risks are mitigated mainly by data representativeness testing? Select TWO.

options.text: Ambiguous data that leads annotators to apply inconsistent labels
Uncontrolled changes to the scripts that make up the data pipeline
A numeric attribute that contains values of the wrong data type
Training data that focuses on a subset of all the intended use cases
An imbalanced dataset that covers some target classes insufficiently

questions.explanation: Imbalanced classes and data focused on a subset of use cases are listed against data representativeness testing, together with augmentation skew, missing data and uncovered value ranges. Wrong data types call for dataset constraint testing, ambiguous labels for label correctness testing and uncontrolled pipeline changes for data pipeline testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.1 (p. 47); AI-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which example illustrates algorithmic bias rather than data bias?

options.text: An attacker deliberately inserted manipulated loan applications into the training dataset before training
The training data for a loan system was collected in one region and underrepresents the applicants who live in other regions
A loan system applies a fixed credit-score decision threshold that systematically disadvantages one group of applicants
Historical loan decisions used as training labels reflect the unfair practices of past human loan officers

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias comes from defects within the algorithm, model or development framework that introduce systemic unfairness, such as a credit-score decision threshold. Unrepresentative data, historical skews and deliberate poisoning are sources of data bias. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); AI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: During system testing of a data pipeline, testers deliberately feed corrupted and malformed records into it. What is the purpose of this fault injection testing?

options.text: To measure the model's accuracy on corrupted records so that the acceptance criteria can be lowered for noisy production data streams
To measure the pipeline's robustness by assessing whether it maintains data integrity when faced with unexpected or corrupted data
To compare the pipeline with the previous release so that A/B testing can choose the faster version for production use
To generate additional labelled training data so that the model learns to classify corrupted records correctly in operation

questions.explanation: Fault injection testing during system testing simulates defective data inputs to assess whether the pipeline maintains data integrity with unexpected or corrupted data. It is not meant to lower acceptance criteria, create training data or compare release speed. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); AI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team starts data representativeness testing for a speech-recognition model. What should be done FIRST?

options.text: Define the target population by analysing use cases, users and environments, and create a stratified reference baseline
Run Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests between the training data and the test data to compare all of their individual feature distributions
Remove all edge cases from the training data so that its distributions match the typical operational data
Train the model and compare its accuracy for each accent with the accuracy reported by competing products

questions.explanation: Representativeness testing starts by defining the target population: understanding use cases and operational context, identifying expected distributions and edge cases, and applying stratified sampling to create a reference baseline. Statistical comparisons follow, testing should happen before training, and edge cases must be covered. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.4 (p. 50); AI-5.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt:
A marathon results dataset has the attributes runner_id, age, half_time_min (time at halfway) and finish_time_min. One constraint requires finish_time_min to be greater than half_time_min for every runner. Given these records:
R1: runner_id 1001, age 34, half_time_min 101, finish_time_min 215
R2: runner_id 1002, age 7, half_time_min 95, finish_time_min 198
R3: runner_id 1003, age 41, half_time_min 128, finish_time_min 121
R4: runner_id 1003, age 52, half_time_min 110, finish_time_min 236
Which record violates this comparison constraint?

options.text: R1
R4
R3
R2

questions.explanation: The greater-than comparison constraint requires finish_time_min > half_time_min; R3 has a finish time of 121, below its halfway time of 128. R2 might break an age range constraint and R4 repeats runner_id 1003, which a duplicate constraint would flag, but neither violates the comparison constraint. R1 satisfies all of these rules. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.5 (p. 51); AI-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Three annotators independently label the same 1,000 medical images, and Cohen's Kappa between them is low. What does this MOST LIKELY indicate?

options.text: Defects in the labelling guidelines, ambiguous data or poor annotation that need investigation
Data drift in production, because operational images differ from those in the original training set
A missing range constraint, because Kappa measures values outside their allowed ranges
Overfitting of the model, because the model learned from the labels of only one annotator

questions.explanation: In multiple annotation, data points are labelled by several annotators and compared; inter-annotator agreement measured with Cohen's Kappa or percentage agreement that is low can indicate defects in labelling guidelines, ambiguous data or poor annotation. Overfitting, drift and range constraints are unrelated to annotator agreement. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.6 (p. 52); AI-5.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrained recommendation model may perform worse than the current version on agreed metrics. Which mitigation does the model risk table give for this risk?

options.text: A/B testing
Model documentation review
Smoke testing
Fuzz testing

questions.explanation: Model updates that decrease ML functional performance are mitigated by A/B testing against the existing variant. Smoke testing addresses immediate deployment failures, fuzz testing addresses robustness to unexpected inputs, and documentation review addresses poor documentation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.1 (p. 55); AI-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are aims of reviewing ML model documentation against a checklist? Select TWO.

options.text: Replacing ML functional performance testing of the model
Measuring the model's inference latency on the target device
Verifying that the relevant regulatory requirements have been met
Identifying missing, inaccurate or inconsistent information
Retraining the model using the documentation as training data

questions.explanation: Reviewing documentation aims to identify missing, inaccurate or inconsistent information, improve clarity and maintainability, provide enough information for test and deployment, and verify that regulatory requirements are met. It does not train the model, replace performance testing or measure latency. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.2 (p. 56); AI-6.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An acceptance criterion states a target accuracy, a margin of error and a confidence level. If the confidence level is kept fixed while more test cases are run, what happens?

options.text: The margin of error decreases, so the test result becomes more precise
The margin of error increases, so the result needs a larger tolerance
The confidence level decreases, so the test result becomes less certain
The target accuracy increases, so the criterion becomes harder to meet

questions.explanation: With more tests, either the confidence level is fixed and the margin of error decreases (more precise), or the margin of error is fixed and the confidence level increases (more certain). The target accuracy is part of the requirement and does not change with the number of tests. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.3 (p. 57); AI-6.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is an adversarial example?

options.text: A test input created by a red team to make an LLM reveal confidential training data through a long multi-turn conversation
A slightly modified version of a legitimate input, often imperceptible to humans, that causes the model to make an incorrect prediction
A legitimate input from a rare class that the model has not seen during training and therefore classifies with an unusually low confidence
A training example whose label was changed by an attacker before training, so the model learns an incorrect association

questions.explanation: Adversarial testing provides perturbations to inputs, often imperceptible to humans, designed to cause incorrect predictions; successful ones are adversarial examples. A rare legitimate input is not adversarial, extracting training data through dialogue is a red-teaming attack, and relabelling training data is data poisoning. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.4 (p. 58); AI-6.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A route-planning system computes the shortest driving distance on a road network in which every road can be driven in both directions. A source test case from Ashford to Brook returned 12.4 km and was judged correct. Which follow-up test case and expected result apply a valid metamorphic relation?

options.text: Close a road that is not on the original Ashford to Brook route and expect a distance below 12.4 km
Add a new road between Ashford and a nearby village and expect a distance greater than 12.4 km
Swap the start and destination (Brook to Ashford) and expect the same distance of 12.4 km
Plan a route from Brook to a different town and expect a distance of exactly 12.4 km

questions.explanation: On a network where every road is two-way, the shortest distance is symmetric, so swapping start and destination must give the same 12.4 km. Adding a road can only keep or shorten the shortest route, closing an unused road should leave the distance unchanged, and an unrelated town pair has no relation to the source output. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.5 (p. 59); AI-6.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: New financial regulations reclassify a transaction type from 'low-risk' to 'high-risk', although the transactions themselves look the same as before. Which kind of drift is this?

options.text: Label drift, because annotators disagreed when labelling the historical transactions in the training data
Model drift, because the model's weights changed when the new regulations were published
Concept drift, because the relationship between the input data and the correct output has changed
Data drift, because the statistical properties of the operational input data have changed

questions.explanation: Concept drift occurs when the relationship between input data and the correct output changes, as when new regulations change what 'high-risk' means for the same transactions. Data drift is a change in the input distribution; the syllabus does not define the other two terms. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.7 (p. 60); AI-6.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A model scores 97% on the validation dataset but 79% on a separate test dataset that includes some less common examples. What does this suggest?

options.text: The model may be overfitting, because it performs significantly worse on unseen test data than on validation data
The test dataset may be defective, because a correct model scores the same on every dataset
The model may be underfitting, because the results are high on both validation and test data
The model may be drifting, because operational data has changed since it was deployed

questions.explanation: Overfitting is tested by evaluating performance on a separate test dataset not used in training, including less common examples; significantly worse results than on validation data suggest overfitting. Underfitting gives low results on training and validation, scores are not expected to be identical, and the model has not been deployed. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.8 (p. 60); AI-6.1.8 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes A/B testing in the context of ML systems?

options.text: One variant is run with original and modified inputs, and a relation between the outputs is checked
