Two versions are compared, one of which acts as a pseudo-oracle, to find defects in the cases where their outputs disagree
One variant is released to a small group of users, and the rollout stops if its error rate increases
Two variants receive the same inputs and their responses are compared statistically to decide which variant is better

questions.explanation: A/B testing compares how two variants respond to the same inputs to determine which is better, using statistical techniques over multiple runs. Using a pseudo-oracle to find defects is back-to-back testing, checking relations is metamorphic testing, and limited release is canary testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.9 (p. 61); AI-6.1.9 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why should the pseudo-oracle in back-to-back testing ideally avoid sharing software components with the system under test?

options.text: Shared components could contain the same defect, so both might give matching outputs even when both are wrong
Shared components would require the same hardware, so the pseudo-oracle could not run in the test environment
Shared components would give the pseudo-oracle access to the test inputs, so the comparison would no longer be blind
Shared components would make the pseudo-oracle too slow, so the comparison could not run within the test schedule

questions.explanation: If the pseudo-oracle and the system under test share components, both might contain the same defect and produce matching but incorrect outputs; this is a particular concern with reused open-source AI components. Speed, blindness and hardware are not the reason given. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.10 (p. 62); AI-6.1.10 (K2).

questions.prompt: After a framework upgrade, the reported F1-score of an unchanged model rises by 3%. Which mitigation does the syllabus give for the risk of a defective evaluation implementation in the framework?

options.text: Review the framework's evaluation code and cross-check its results, for example against manual benchmark calculations
Retrain the model with more epochs so that the new F1-score is confirmed by the next full training run of the framework
Run canary testing on 5% of production traffic and accept the higher F1-score if user complaints do not increase
Perform usability testing of the framework so that data scientists can read the evaluation report more easily

questions.explanation: Defective implementation of evaluation by the framework is mitigated by reviewing the framework's evaluation code and cross-checking its results, for example against manual benchmarks. Canary testing, retraining and usability testing do not reveal whether the metric is calculated correctly. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.1 (p. 64); AI-7.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes shadow testing from canary testing?

options.text: In shadow testing the old model is removed before the new one starts; in canary testing both models answer every request for comparison
In shadow testing the new model processes live requests without affecting responses; in canary testing a small share of users is actually served by it
In shadow testing a small share of users is served by the new model; in canary testing the new model runs offline on historical data alone
In shadow testing the new model is tested on a mobile device; in canary testing it is tested on cloud servers and edge devices

questions.explanation: Shadow testing runs the new model in parallel with the production model on the same live requests without affecting live responses; canary testing releases the updated model to a small subset of production traffic, such as 5% of users, and monitors real-time metrics. The other options swap or misdescribe the two. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.2 (p. 65); AI-7.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A bank replaces its rule-based loan-approval engine with a deep learning model. Which new testing concern follows MOST directly from this change?

options.text: The bank no longer needs to monitor the system after release because learned behavior cannot change
Explaining why a particular application was rejected becomes harder because the decision logic is not visible as explicit rules
Approval decisions become fully repeatable because a trained model removes the need for statistical testing
Test cases can no longer use the loan application form as a test basis because the model has no requirements

questions.explanation: Deep models can contain very many parameters, so understanding why a decision was made (explainability) becomes a key challenge, particularly in finance. Requirements and forms remain a test basis, AI outputs are not always predictable, and adaptive behavior needs continuous monitoring. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); AI-1.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A vendor claims its frontier large language model is 'general AI' because it can write code, summarise contracts and answer quiz questions. How should a tester classify the model according to the CT-AI syllabus?

options.text: As narrow AI, because frontier models are a subset of narrow AI that remains task-specific despite advanced capabilities
As symbolic AI, because a model that produces code must be based on explicitly programmed logical rules
As general AI, because any model that performs several different language tasks has the versatility of a human
As super AI, because a frontier model trained on internet-scale data surpasses human intelligence in all intellectual domains

questions.explanation: Frontier AI is the most advanced form of narrow AI: large, highly autonomous GenAI systems that remain task-specific and have not achieved the versatility of general AI. No system today has general intelligence, super AI is hypothetical, and LLMs are not rule-based. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.2 (p. 15); AI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between machine learning, deep learning and generative AI?

options.text: Deep learning is a subset of ML that uses deep neural networks, and generative AI builds on such technologies to create new content
Deep learning and ML are separate branches of AI, and generative AI is a rule-based approach that uses neither of them
ML is a subset of deep learning, and generative AI is the name for any ML model that predicts a numerical value
Generative AI is the parent field, and ML and deep learning are two independent techniques for producing text and images

questions.explanation: ML is a core branch of AI; deep learning is a subset of ML methods using deep neural networks; GenAI builds on these technologies, such as transformers in LLMs, to create content. The other options invert or misstate the hierarchy, and predicting a number is ML regression. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); AI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which technology generates content by gradually adding noise to data and then learning to remove it?

options.text: Recurrent neural networks
Diffusion models
Generative adversarial networks
Support vector machines

questions.explanation: Diffusion models generate content by gradually adding and then removing noise, which produces high-quality outputs. GANs use two competing networks, RNNs process sequences, and SVMs are a classical ML technique, not a generative mechanism. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.4 (p. 17); AI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are typical functions provided by ML development frameworks? Select TWO.

options.text: Negotiating licence terms for training data with third-party data providers
Defining the business acceptance criteria that stakeholders agree for the model
Converting a trained model into a format suitable for mobile or edge devices
Loading, cleaning and transforming the data used to train and test a model
Writing the regulatory conformity assessment required for high-risk systems

questions.explanation: Frameworks provide data handling, model building, training and optimisation, evaluation and, in some cases, deployment, such as converting models for web, mobile, edge or embedded targets. Licensing, acceptance criteria and regulatory documentation are organisational activities, not framework functions. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.7 (p. 19); AI-1.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does the EU AI Act affect the testing of AI-based systems?

options.text: It categorises systems by risk, and high-risk systems face stringent requirements including rigorous testing, data governance and human oversight
It applies only to AI systems developed inside the EU, so testing requirements depend on the developer's location
It requires the same level of testing for all AI-based systems, from spam filters to medical devices, regardless of risk
It replaces technical standards such as ISO/IEC TR 29119-11, so testers no longer need guidance documents

questions.explanation: The EU AI Act takes a risk-based approach, categorising systems from minimal to unacceptable risk, with stringent requirements for high-risk systems backed by fines based on global turnover. Requirements are tailored by risk, technical standards complement regulation, and the statements about scope are not in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.8 (p. 20); AI-1.1.8 (K2).

questions.prompt: A security operator can stop an AI-controlled warehouse vehicle in time to prevent a collision with a worker. Which ISO/IEC 25059 characteristic is MOST directly involved?

options.text: AI robustness
Intervenability
Functional adaptability
Transparency

questions.explanation: Intervenability, a new sub-characteristic of security, is the degree to which an operator can intervene in an AI-based system's functioning in a timely manner to prevent harm or hazard. Transparency concerns communicated information, adaptability concerns autonomous change, and robustness concerns maintaining correctness under adverse conditions. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.1 (p. 22); AI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A medical-device team cannot trace each requirement to the code that implements it, because the desired behavior was implied by labelled training images. Which AI safety challenge does this illustrate?

options.text: Non-determinism
Evolving regulations
Specifications
Explainability and transparency

questions.explanation: Requirements for many AI-based systems begin as vague goals implicitly provided through training data, so traceability from requirements to implementation can be inadequate. Non-determinism concerns variable behavior, evolving regulations concern changing standards, and explainability concerns understanding decisions. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.2 (p. 23); AI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion is an example for AI robustness?

options.text: The approval rates of the loan model do not differ between age groups by more than the agreed fairness threshold
The API returns the unique version identifier of the deployed model and a link to its documentation
Prediction response time stays below 1 second while access to the central vulnerability database is disrupted for 30 seconds
A supervisor can take control of an autonomous drone within 0.5 seconds after it reports a lost GPS position

questions.explanation: AI robustness is about maintaining performance despite adverse conditions such as external disruption. The version endpoint is transparency, taking control of the drone is user controllability, and the fairness threshold belongs to societal and ethical risk mitigation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); AI-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about ML regression is correct?

options.text: It groups unlabelled data points into regions, and it is used for targeted marketing based on customers' purchasing behavior
It predicts which predefined class an input belongs to, and it is the supervised counterpart of clustering for labelled categories
It predicts continuous numerical values, and the term is unrelated to the regression of other ISTQB syllabi, which concerns change-related defects
It re-runs earlier test cases after a model update, as regression testing, to confirm the retrained model has no new defects

questions.explanation: ML regression is a supervised learning task that predicts continuous values such as age or stock prices; the syllabus notes that it differs from regression in other ISTQB syllabi. Assigning predefined classes is classification, re-running tests is regression testing, and grouping unlabelled data is clustering. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.1 (p. 27); AI-3.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly classifies two settings passed to an ML algorithm?

options.text: The number of layers in a neural network is a data preparation step; the number of training iterations is a deployment setting
The number of layers in a neural network is a learned weight; the number of training iterations is a confusion-matrix value
The number of layers in a neural network is a model hyperparameter; the number of training iterations is an algorithm hyperparameter
The number of layers in a neural network is an algorithm hyperparameter; the number of training iterations is a model hyperparameter

questions.explanation: Parameters that define the model structure, such as the number of layers or the depth of a decision tree, are model hyperparameters; parameters that control training, such as the number of iterations, are algorithm hyperparameters. Weights are learned, not passed in, and the other options mix in unrelated activities. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.2 (p. 28); AI-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO activities belong to data acquisition? Select TWO.

options.text: Augmenting the data with synthetic and adversarial examples
Extracting a smaller set of informative, non-redundant features
Normalising numeric data so that features share a common scale
Labelling data for supervised learning and checking label consistency
Gathering data from databases, APIs and real-time sensors

questions.explanation: Data acquisition covers identifying relevant data types, gathering data from diverse sources and labelling data for supervised learning. Normalising and augmenting are preprocessing activities, and extracting informative features is feature engineering. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.2.1 (p. 31); AI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which description of k-fold cross-validation is correct?

options.text: The model is trained k times on all the data with different random seeds, and the fold with the highest accuracy becomes the test dataset
The data is split into k folds; each fold serves once as validation data while the model trains on the other k-1 folds, and the fold results are averaged
The data is split into k folds; the model is trained on one fold and validated on the remaining k-1 folds, and only the best single fold result is reported
The data is split into k test sets that are each used once after deployment to monitor the deployed model's operational performance

questions.explanation: In k-fold cross-validation the data is divided into k folds; for each fold, the model trains on the k-1 other folds and is validated on the held-out fold, and the metrics are averaged. Training on one fold, picking the best result or using folds after deployment does not match the technique. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.2.3 (p. 32); AI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt:
A fraud classifier is tested on 1,000 transactions. Note how the confusion matrix counts are grouped:
Actual fraud: predicted fraud 120, predicted legit 30
Actual legit: predicted fraud 40, predicted legit 810
What is the precision of the classifier?
questions.explanation: Here the counts are grouped by actual class: TP = 120, FN = 30, FP = 40, TN = 810. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 120 / 160 = 75.0%. 80.0% is recall, 120 / 150; 93.0% is accuracy, 930 / 1,000; and 77.4% is the F1-score. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.3.1 (p. 33); AI-3.3.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: During training of a deep neural network, what happens to the error (loss) between the generated output and the known correct result?

options.text: It is added to the network's input layer so that the next example compensates for the previous mistake
It is used to choose a different activation function for each layer after every training example
It is fed back through the network to adjust the weights and biases so that the difference is reduced
It is stored as a new neuron in the network's output layer so that later predictions can be corrected

questions.explanation: Training compares the network's output with the correct result, and the resulting error is fed back to adjust weights and biases, minimising the difference over many passes. Training does not add neurons, change activation functions per example, or alter inputs. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.4.1 (p. 36); AI-3.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does neuron coverage measure for a neural network?

options.text: The proportion of neurons whose output range sections are each reached during testing
The proportion of hidden layers whose weights have been changed by the latest training run
The proportion of neurons whose output leaves the range observed during their training
The proportion of neurons whose output exceeds a specified threshold during testing

questions.explanation: Neuron coverage is the proportion of neurons with outputs above a specified threshold during testing. Reaching sections of each neuron's output range is k-multisection neuron coverage, leaving the trained range is neuron boundary coverage, and weight changes are not a coverage measure. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.4.3 (p. 37); AI-3.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An LLM-based chatbot runs with fixed weights in production but is replaced by an updated model every quarter. How does the CT-AI syllabus position such a system?

options.text: Fully adaptive, because any model that is updated more than once a year is adaptive
Fully locked, because chatbots never change their behavior after initial deployment
Between fully locked and fully adaptive: locked at runtime but updated periodically
Outside the continuum, because GenAI systems are neither locked nor adaptive systems

questions.explanation: Many GenAI systems such as LLM-based chatbots are deployed as locked models at runtime but are updated periodically, placing them between fully locked and fully adaptive. Systems span a continuum, so GenAI is not outside it, and periodic updates do not make a system fully adaptive. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.1 (p. 39); AI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A delivery-route model was trained on data from one city but will operate in several regions. Which reason for statistical testing does this situation illustrate?

options.text: Regulatory and safety context: route models are high-risk, so statistics replace the need to test in every region
Handling uncertainty and bias: statistical tests reveal the model's internal weights, so all regions can be compared
Non-determinism: the model produces the same output for identical inputs, so testing one route per region is enough
Distributional performance evaluation: training data differs from the data met in use, so a significant sample of real scenarios is needed

questions.explanation: AI models are trained on specific data distributions that do not exactly match operation, so a statistically significant sample from the relevant operational distributions must be tested. The other options misstate non-determinism, overstate the regulatory point, or claim statistics expose internal weights. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.2 (p. 40); AI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: For each test run of a drone's landing model, testers fix the wind speed, lighting level and network latency so that outputs are predictable and repeatable. Which oracle approach is this?

options.text: Using a proxy oracle
Consulting independent domain experts
Defining environmental boundaries
Defining output boundaries

questions.explanation: Defining environmental boundaries means specifying test-environment conditions such as lighting, temperature or network latency to make outputs predictable and repeatable. Output boundaries specify acceptable output ranges, proxy oracles use secondary systems, and expert consultation relies on human judgement. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.3 (p. 40); AI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team uses an image-recognition system to check automatically whether images produced by a GenAI system show the requested objects. What caution does the syllabus give?

options.text: A second AI system makes the test fully deterministic, so the results of the test do not need statistical analysis
A second AI system cannot evaluate images, so generated images must be reviewed manually in each case
A second AI system used as an oracle may reproduce similar biases or errors, so it should be used carefully
A second AI system must be trained on the same data as the GenAI system, so its results agree with it

questions.explanation: The syllabus allows a second GenAI system to determine test results automatically, for example an image recognition system checking generated images, but warns that such approaches may reproduce similar biases or errors. The other options contradict this or claim guaranteed agreement. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.1 (p. 41); AI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An HR assistant answers employee questions using RAG over internal policy documents. You are red-teaming it for security before release. Which activity BEST targets an AI-specific security vulnerability?

options.text: Place a policy document containing hidden instructions in the test retrieval corpus and check whether the assistant follows them
Run a public reasoning benchmark on the policy documents and compare the score with the previous model version
Monitor live employee prompts after release and block prompts that match a list of known attack patterns
Measure the response time of the assistant while 500 simulated employees send policy questions at once

questions.explanation: Security red teaming looks for vulnerabilities to external attacks, including AI-specific ones such as indirect prompt injection and malicious content hidden in RAG documents. Benchmarks are static comparisons, filtering live prompts is blue teaming, and response time under load is performance testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.2 (p. 42); AI-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A system calls a third-party AI service to classify customer emails. At which test level is API testing of this service performed?

options.text: Operational acceptance testing
Input data testing
System integration testing
Component integration testing

questions.explanation: Where AI is provided as a service, API testing of that service is performed as part of component integration testing, together with checking that predictions are exchanged and used correctly. Input data and model testing target data and models, and system integration testing covers external systems in an operationally representative environment. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.1 (p. 43); AI-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A recruitment model was trained on ten years of hiring data in which one group was rarely hired. How should this risk be categorised using the ML workflow areas?

options.text: As a deployment risk and a product risk: model API incompatibility
As a model risk and a project risk: an overfitted hiring model
As an input data risk and a product risk: biased training data
As a development risk and a project risk: poor framework choice

questions.explanation: Biased training data is an example of a product risk in the input data area, alongside data-pipeline defects and unrepresentative training data. Framework choice is a development risk, overfitting is a model risk, and API incompatibility is not the issue described. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.2 (p. 44); AI-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team suspects that a competitor has injected manipulated records into a public dataset used for training. Which set of mitigations does the CT-AI syllabus associate with poisoned training data?

options.text: A/B testing, data provenance testing, exploratory data analysis and attacks as part of red teaming
Label correctness testing, multiple annotation, model loss analysis and model confidence score analysis
Installability testing, rollback testing, canary testing and cross-device testing of the model
Requirements review, usability testing, accessibility testing and localisation testing of the UI

questions.explanation: The syllabus maps poisoned training data to A/B testing, data provenance testing, EDA and attacks as part of red teaming. Label-focused approaches address annotation problems, deployment tests address releases, and the last set targets conventional user-interface concerns. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.1 (p. 47); AI-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In disparate impact analysis, what is a counterfactual?

options.text: A copy of a realistic example in which the label is removed so the model must predict it without supervision
A copy of a realistic example in which the expected output is fixed by a domain expert before the test is run on the model
A copy of a realistic example in which every attribute is randomised to test the model's robustness to noise
A copy of a realistic example in which only a sensitive attribute is changed, such as gender in a loan application

questions.explanation: Disparate impact analysis generates counterfactuals for sensitive attributes, for example changing gender from male to female in a loan application, and checks whether the model's result changes. Removing labels, randomising all attributes or fixing expected outputs are not counterfactuals. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); AI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why does system testing of a data pipeline include back-to-back testing of the operational pipeline against the training pipeline?

options.text: To verify that the operational pipeline uses different libraries, so that a shared defect cannot occur in either pipeline
To verify that the training pipeline is faster, so that the operational pipeline can be replaced by the training pipeline in the production environment
To verify that the training pipeline has more test cases, so that its test suite can be reused for component testing
To verify that both pipelines process the same raw data consistently, so the model receives production data prepared like its training data

questions.explanation: Back-to-back testing compares the operational pipeline with the training pipeline to verify consistent functionality, since the model's performance depends on production data being prepared in the same way as training data. Speed, test-suite size and library choice are not the purpose. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); AI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statistical tests does the CT-AI syllabus mention for comparing the distributions of a training dataset with representative reference data?

options.text: t-test and Mann-Whitney U test
Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Cohen's Kappa and percentage agreement
Confusion matrix and F1-score

questions.explanation: Representativeness testing uses formal statistical tests such as Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov to compare distributions. The t-test and Mann-Whitney U are listed for A/B testing, Cohen's Kappa for inter-annotator agreement, and confusion-matrix metrics for classification performance. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.4 (p. 50); AI-5.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt:
For a hotel booking dataset, the following constraints are defined:
i. No two bookings share the same booking reference
ii. The nightly room price is between 20 and 2,000
iii. The check-out date is later than the check-in date
iv. A minimum of 10,000 bookings have a non-null guest email address
Which classification of the constraints is correct?

options.text: i duplicate (multi-value), ii range (single-value), iii greater than (comparison), iv count (multi-value)
i duplicate (single-value), ii range (multi-value), iii correlate (comparison), iv sum (multi-value)
i useful (multi-value), ii type (single-value), iii greater than (comparison), iv count (single-value)
i duplicate (multi-value), ii outlier (multi-value), iii correlate (comparison), iv missing (single-value)

questions.explanation: A unique booking reference is a duplicate constraint across instances; a price range is a single-value range constraint; check-out after check-in compares two attributes with greater than; and a minimum number of non-null values is a count constraint over many instances. The distractors misclassify the constraint type or its scope. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.5 (p. 51); AI-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: During training, some data points keep a very high loss: the model's predictions for them deviate strongly from their assigned labels. Which label correctness approach uses this information?

options.text: Data distribution analysis, because high loss shows the model's label distribution differs from similar datasets
Automated rule-based testing, because high loss shows that bounding boxes extend beyond image boundaries
Model loss analysis, because consistently high loss can indicate that those data points are mislabelled
Multiple annotation, because high loss shows that the annotators of those points disagreed with each other

questions.explanation: Model loss analysis treats data points with high loss during training as candidates for mislabelling, since the model struggles to learn the assigned label. Multiple annotation, distribution comparison and rule-based checks use other evidence. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.6 (p. 52); AI-5.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A game-playing agent achieves a high score by exploiting a flaw in its scoring rules rather than by playing well. Which model risk and mitigation does this illustrate?

options.text: Concept drift, mitigated by drift testing
Overfitting, mitigated by testing for overfitting and underfitting
Reward hacking, mitigated by reward hacking testing
Side-effects, mitigated by smoke testing

questions.explanation: Exploiting the reward mechanism instead of achieving the intended goal is reward hacking, which the model risk table maps to reward hacking testing. Concept drift concerns changing input-output relationships, overfitting concerns generalisation, and side-effects are mitigated by side-effects testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.1 (p. 55); AI-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts Model Cards with Datasheets for Datasets?

options.text: Model Cards are regulatory approvals issued under the EU AI Act; Datasheets are the vendor's marketing summaries of the model and its datasets
Model Cards list the hyperparameters chosen during model tuning; Datasheets list the hardware and cloud services used for training and inference
Model Cards describe a dataset's motivation, composition and collection process; Datasheets summarise a model's evaluation results, limits and ethical risks
Model Cards summarise a model's intended uses, evaluation results and ethics; Datasheets describe a dataset's motivation, composition, collection and uses

questions.explanation: Model Cards provide concise overviews of a model's intended uses, evaluation results and ethical considerations; Datasheets for Datasets offer standardised formats describing datasets, including motivation, composition, collection process and uses. The distractors swap or misdescribe the two frameworks. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.2 (p. 56); AI-6.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which properties must the test dataset have for ML functional performance testing of a probabilistic model?

options.text: It is generated from the training dataset by augmentation, so that it contains the same distributions
It contains edge cases alone, so that the model is tested where it is most likely to fail in operation
It is large, independent of the training and validation datasets, and representative of the operational input domain
It is small and reused from the validation dataset, so that results can be compared with tuning results

questions.explanation: Validating statistical criteria requires a large test dataset that is completely independent of training and validation data and is a representative sample of the operational input domain. Reusing validation data, deriving tests from training data or testing only edge cases would distort the estimate. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.3 (p. 57); AI-6.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester has no access to a model's internals. How can adversarial test inputs be created using a black-box approach based on transferability?

options.text: Read the original model's weights from its deployment package and calculate the decision boundary directly
Build an equivalent model whose inner workings are known, craft adversarial inputs for it, and apply them to the original model
Ask the model's developers for the training data and replay it with small changes to each training label
Retrain the original model with adversarial inputs so that it reveals its decision boundary during inference

questions.explanation: Black-box adversarial testing can create an equivalent model with known internals, generate adversarial inputs from it and, assuming equivalent models share classification boundaries (transferability), apply them to the original model. Reading weights is white-box, and retraining or relabelling does not test the original model. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.4 (p. 58); AI-6.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A search engine returned 120 results for the query 'test automation tools', and this source test case passed. Using a metamorphic relation based on adding a mandatory term, which follow-up test case is appropriate?

options.text: Search for 'test automation tools AND python' and expect exactly 120 results
Search for 'garden furniture AND python' and expect no more than 120 results
Search for 'test automation tools AND python' and expect no more than 120 results
Search for 'test automation tools AND python' and expect clearly more than 120 results

questions.explanation: Adding a mandatory term narrows the query, so the follow-up result count must not exceed the source count of 120. Requiring exactly 120 or more than 120 contradicts the relation, and a query with different base terms has no relation to the source test case. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.5 (p. 59); AI-6.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team has no ground truth for its model's recent predictions. Which drift testing approach can it still use?

options.text: Back-to-back drift testing, comparing the model's predictions with those of an identical model
Static drift testing, comparing input and predicted-output distributions with a test such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Shadow drift testing, routing the requests to the training pipeline instead of the live model
Dynamic drift testing, comparing user feedback with the model's predictions against a threshold

questions.explanation: Static drift testing does not depend on current ground truth; it compares statistical properties of the input and predicted-output distributions, for example with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Dynamic drift testing needs ground truth from user feedback, and the other two are not drift-testing approaches. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.7 (p. 60); AI-6.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which observation suggests that a model is underfitting?

options.text: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are consistently low on both the training and the validation datasets
Accuracy is high on the validation dataset but falls slowly after deployment as the users' behavior gradually changes
Accuracy is high on all datasets, but the model's predictions differ from a pseudo-oracle's outputs
Accuracy is very high on the training dataset but much lower on the independent test dataset

questions.explanation: Underfitting is indicated when ML functional performance metrics are consistently low on both training and validation sets. A large drop on unseen data indicates overfitting, a slow fall after deployment indicates drift, and differences from a pseudo-oracle are back-to-back testing findings. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.8 (p. 60); AI-6.1.8 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about A/B testing and test design is correct?

options.text: A/B testing generates test cases automatically from the training data and the expected results of the model
A/B testing designs test cases from metamorphic relations, so it needs no operational inputs at all
A/B testing derives test cases from the confusion matrix, so the test basis is the model's error rate
A/B testing does not generate test cases or guide their design, although operational inputs are often used in the tests

questions.explanation: A/B testing addresses the oracle problem by using the existing system as a partial test oracle, but it does not generate test cases or guide test design, although operational inputs are often incorporated. The other statements attribute test-design capabilities that A/B testing does not have. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.9 (p. 61); AI-6.1.9 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is needed to run functional back-to-back tests between a new ML system and a pseudo-oracle?

options.text: Expected results alone, because the pseudo-oracle generates the test inputs from its own operational logs
Test inputs, for example from existing regression suites or generated from training data, but no expected results
Test inputs and expected results for each case, because the pseudo-oracle cannot generate its own outputs for comparison
A labelled confusion matrix for each test case, because back-to-back testing compares classification metrics

questions.explanation: Back-to-back testing requires only generating test inputs, not expected results, since the pseudo-oracle provides the comparison point; inputs can come from regression suites or be generated from training data. Comparing aggregated metrics is closer to A/B testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.10 (p. 62); AI-6.1.10 (K2).

questions.prompt: A new model is ready but may be no improvement over the current production model. Which mitigation does the ML development risk table give?

options.text: Installability testing
Framework documentation review
Label correctness testing
Shadow testing

questions.explanation: The risk that a deployed model is no improvement over the current model is mitigated by shadow testing, which runs both models on the same live requests without affecting responses. The other tests address installation, labels and framework documentation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.1 (p. 64); AI-7.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A network trained in a framework's native format must run on phones, tablets and edge cameras after a format change. Which TWO deployment tests address the risks of this situation MOST directly? Select TWO.

options.text: Shadow testing
Cross-device testing
Canary testing
Rollback testing
Model conversion testing

questions.explanation: Model conversion testing verifies that accuracy, behavior and efficiency are retained after conversion to the deployment format, and cross-device testing verifies correct performance across the intended targets. Shadow, rollback and canary testing address other deployment risks. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.2 (p. 65); AI-7.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why does a self-learning AI-based system need continuous monitoring after deployment, unlike a conventional system?

options.text: Its source code is regenerated after each prediction, so the build pipeline must be rechecked after each release
Its outputs are deterministic on the original hardware alone, so a hardware change invalidates the trained model
Its test basis is deleted after training, so testers must reconstruct requirements from the production logs
Its behavior can keep changing as it encounters new data, so alignment with the core requirements must be checked over time

questions.explanation: Adaptability lets AI-based systems improve with new data, but the same adaptability means behavior drifts from what was tested, so continuous monitoring keeps it aligned with the core requirements. The other options describe mechanisms that the syllabus does not attribute to AI-based systems. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); AI-1.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which description fits super AI as described in the CT-AI syllabus?

options.text: AI that continuously improves itself without human intervention and would surpass human intelligence
AI that requires internet access to function and becomes general AI as soon as it is connected to the web
AI that combines several narrow models in one product, such as translation and speech recognition
AI that performs one task better than any human expert, such as recognising faces in large crowds

questions.explanation: Super AI would keep improving itself without human control and surpass human and general AI; the transition point is called the technological singularity. Superhuman performance on one task is still narrow AI, combining narrow models does not create super AI, and internet access is not strictly required. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.2 (p. 15); AI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A wearable device must recognise spoken commands on a small battery. Which hardware choice is MOST appropriate for running the trained model on the device?

options.text: AI-specific hardware such as a System-on-a-Chip with in-memory processing, with training done in the cloud
A rack of on-premises GPU servers attached to the wearable, because the model needs the same hardware it used in training
A neuromorphic processor used for training, because brain-inspired designs are required for speech recognition
A high-clock-speed general-purpose CPU, because model inference benefits most from complex high-precision operations

questions.explanation: AI-specific solutions such as ASICs and System-on-a-Chip devices are best suited for edge computing, while training is done in the cloud on specialised hardware. Training and inference can use different hardware, CPUs are less efficient for ML, and neuromorphic designs are an emerging architecture, not a requirement. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.5 (p. 18); AI-1.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A start-up has unpredictable demand for its image-tagging service and little capital for hardware. Which hosting option fits BEST?

options.text: Hosting the model on a private cloud, which is the lowest-cost option for workloads with unpredictable peaks
Hosting the model on dedicated on-premises servers, which avoids upfront investment and scales instantly with any change in demand
Hosting the model on the users' smartphones, which provides unlimited hardware capability for large image models
Hosting the model on a public cloud, which offers scalable infrastructure without maintenance and suits fluctuating workloads

questions.explanation: Public cloud hosting provides scalable access to powerful infrastructure, removes maintenance concerns and is ideal for fluctuating workloads with pay-as-you-go pricing. Dedicated servers need significant upfront investment, local hosting has limited hardware, and private clouds add security at a higher cost. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.6 (p. 18); AI-1.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A data science team is choosing between two ML frameworks. Framework 1 has a high-level API; framework 2 has a low-level API. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Framework 1 gives more control over model building but needs more coding expertise, while framework 2 limits customisation
Framework 1 simplifies model creation with fewer customisation options; framework 2 gives more control but needs more coding expertise
Framework 1 can build decision trees and linear models alone, while framework 2 is restricted to building and training deep neural networks
Framework 1 cannot evaluate a trained model on unseen data, while framework 2 cannot deploy a trained model to production

questions.explanation: Lower-level APIs give developers more control over model building but require more coding expertise; higher-level APIs simplify model creation with fewer customisation options. The abstraction level does not restrict a framework to one algorithm family or remove evaluation or deployment functions. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.7 (p. 19); AI-1.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the OECD AI Principles with technical standards such as ISO/IEC TR 29119-11?

options.text: The OECD principles are influential soft law guiding responsible AI strategies, while technical standards give concrete specifications and practices
The OECD principles define test techniques for neural networks, while technical standards define human-centric values
The OECD principles are binding regulation with fines, while technical standards are voluntary marketing statements
The OECD principles replace national AI strategies, while technical standards apply only to safety-critical hardware

questions.explanation: The OECD AI Principles and the UN report on Governing AI for Humanity are soft law instruments that act as a compass for strategies. Standards from ISO and IEEE translate aspirations into concrete technical specifications; for example, ISO/IEC TR 29119-11 gives guidance on testing AI-based systems. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.8 (p. 20); AI-1.1.8 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Given these ISO/IEC 25059 characteristics:
1. AI robustness
2. Transparency
3. User controllability
4. Functional adaptability
And these example measures:
A. Accuracy of a sign-recognition model when images contain heavy fog
B. Time for a fraud analyst to override an automated payment block
C. Time for a music service to reflect a user's newly preferred genre in its suggestions
D. Availability of the deployed model's version identifier and documentation to customers
Which matching is BEST?
questions.explanation: Fog tests whether AI functional correctness is maintained under adverse conditions (robustness); version and documentation information is transparency; overriding an automated decision is user controllability; adapting suggestions to new preferences is functional adaptability. The other matchings swap at least two pairs. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.1 (p. 22); AI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which mitigation does the CT-AI syllabus suggest to prevent a self-learning safety-related system from learning harmful behaviors?

options.text: Disabling safety monitoring after deployment so that observers do not influence the learning process
Increasing the model's temperature setting so that it explores more alternative behaviors during operation
Implementing safety guards, such as a content-moderation component that filters prompts, and managing what and how the model learns
Replacing the training data with synthetic data so that the model cannot learn from operational inputs

questions.explanation: The syllabus suggests managing how the model learns and the data it uses, or implementing safety guards that prevent learning or decisions that compromise safety. Raising temperature increases variability, disabling monitoring removes protection, and synthetic training data does not stop operational learning. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.1.2 (p. 23); AI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why are acceptance criteria for AI-based systems often more difficult to test than those for conventional systems?

options.text: They are defined by the ML framework vendor, so the test team cannot influence their content or thresholds
They are frequently statistical, probabilistic or threshold-based rather than binary, so a single test result cannot show they are met
They must be expressed as source-code assertions, because AI-based systems have no natural-language requirements
They must be written after deployment, because AI behavior is unknown until the system is in production

questions.explanation: For AI-based systems, acceptance criteria often need to be statistical, probabilistic or threshold-based, which means testing must provide sufficient evidence across many cases. They are agreed with stakeholders early (understand the objectives), are not limited to code assertions, and are not set by framework vendors. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); AI-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A supermarket analyses unlabelled till receipts to discover which products are frequently bought together, so that it can recommend related products. Which form of ML does this describe?

options.text: Unsupervised learning using association
Supervised learning using classification
Supervised learning using ML regression
Reinforcement learning using rewards

questions.explanation: Identifying relationships or dependencies among attributes in unlabelled data, such as purchase patterns used for recommendations, is association, a form of unsupervised learning. Classification and ML regression need labelled data, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards for actions. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.1 (p. 27); AI-3.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A model reached 93% accuracy during evaluation, but only 81% when run against the independent test dataset. What does the ML workflow suggest?

options.text: Return to the model generation activities, or even to data preparation, because performance on the test data is significantly lower
Repeat the test with the validation dataset instead, because the evaluation result shows that the test data is defective
Deploy the model now, because the evaluation result is the official measure and the test result merely confirms deployment readiness
Average the two results to 87% and report this to stakeholders as the expected operational accuracy of the deployed model

questions.explanation: If performance with independent test data is significantly lower than during evaluation, it may be necessary to return to model generation, or even to data preparation, to train a new model. The test result, not the evaluation result, verifies the criteria, and averaging or swapping datasets would hide the problem. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.2 (p. 28); AI-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A pretrained image classifier recognises different types of cats. Which adaptation is MOST likely to succeed through fine-tuning?

options.text: Adapting it to translate legal contracts into German
Adapting it to identify dog breeds from photographs
Adapting it to recognise spoken regional accents
Adapting it to forecast monthly electricity prices

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning works best when the new task is similar to the original one; cat breeds to dog breeds is a small change, whereas accents, price forecasting and translation differ greatly in data type and task. The syllabus uses the accent example to show a less effective adaptation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.1.4 (p. 30); AI-3.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about augmentation and sampling during data preprocessing is correct?

options.text: Augmentation increases the number of examples, for example with synthetic data, while sampling uses subsets to reduce training time and cost
Augmentation is performed after deployment to monitor drift, while sampling is performed before deployment to label data
Augmentation removes personal information for privacy, while sampling converts data into a format suitable for the model
Augmentation reduces the dataset by removing outliers, while sampling increases it by duplicating records from minority classes

questions.explanation: Augmenting data increases sample size and can add adversarial examples or synthetic data, whereas sampling subsets reduces training times and computational costs. Removing outliers and anonymising are cleaning activities, format transformation is a separate preprocessing step, and neither augmentation nor sampling is a drift-monitoring activity. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.2.1 (p. 31); AI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A screening model is tested on 500 X-ray images, 50 of which show the condition. The model flags 60 images, and 45 of the flagged images really show the condition. What is the model's F1-score?
questions.explanation: TP = 45, FP = 60 - 45 = 15, FN = 50 - 45 = 5, TN = 500 - 65 = 435. Precision = 45 / 60 = 75.0% and recall = 45 / 50 = 90.0%, so F1 = 2 × 75 × 90 / (75 + 90) = 81.8. 82.5 is the arithmetic mean, not the harmonic mean; 96.0 is accuracy and 75.0 is precision. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.3.1 (p. 33); AI-3.3.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: What does the term 'epoch' mean when training a neural network?

options.text: One hidden layer added to the network to improve accuracy
One pass of the entire training dataset through the network
One training example processed by a single neuron of the network
One adjustment of the learning rate during training

questions.explanation: Each pass through the training dataset is called an epoch; weights and biases are gradually adjusted over successive epochs. The other options describe a single example, a structural change or a hyperparameter change. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.4.1 (p. 36); AI-3.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester reports low neuron boundary coverage (NBC) for an image classifier. What does this indicate?

options.text: Few neurons produced outputs above the specified activation threshold during the test runs
Few neurons produced outputs above their training maximum or below their training minimum during testing
Few sections of each neuron's divided output range were activated during the test runs
Few test images were classified correctly compared with the images in the training dataset

questions.explanation: NBC is the proportion of neurons whose output during testing exceeds the maximum or falls below the minimum achieved in training, so low NBC means tests rarely push neurons beyond trained behavior. The other options describe neuron coverage, kMNC and accuracy. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 3.4.3 (p. 37); AI-3.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A locked image-recognition model is retrained with new data and redeployed. How should the updated model be treated for testing?

options.text: As a new system that needs a fresh round of testing, because its weights and biases have changed
As an adaptive system, so testing is replaced by monitoring of the live predictions after release
As the same system, so only the user interface needs regression testing after the redeployment
As a validated system, so the previous test results remain valid if the accuracy stays above 90%

questions.explanation: An updated locked AI-based system is typically considered a new system, and a fresh round of testing is required. Retraining changes the learned behavior, so previous results do not carry over and monitoring does not replace testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.1 (p. 39); AI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements give reasons for a statistical approach to testing AI-based systems? Select TWO.

options.text: Statistical testing removes the test oracle problem, because averages replace the need for expected results
Deterministic models require larger samples than probabilistic models to reach statistical significance
The same inputs may not always yield the same output, so many test runs are needed for significant results
Regulated industries may require evidence that safety or fairness thresholds are met with high confidence
Statistical testing replaces acceptance criteria, because a confidence level defines the business goal

questions.explanation: Non-determinism and the regulatory and safety context are two of the reasons listed in the syllabus, together with distributional performance evaluation and handling uncertainty and bias. Statistics do not remove the oracle problem or replace acceptance criteria, and deterministic systems do not need larger samples. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.2 (p. 40); AI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team has no expected results for a large set of unlabelled inputs. It trains a separate model on labelled data and uses that model's predictions to assess the outputs of the system under test. Which approach is the team using?

options.text: A metamorphic relation
A proxy oracle
An environmental boundary
A ground-truth label set

questions.explanation: A proxy oracle uses secondary systems or models, including other AI systems, to assess outputs when direct expected results are unavailable, such as a proxy model trained on labelled data to predict for unlabelled tests. Metamorphic testing derives follow-up tests, environmental boundaries fix conditions, and the unlabelled inputs have no ground truth. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.1.3 (p. 40); AI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of benchmark suites when testing GenAI models?

options.text: To provide standardised, curated datasets and tasks so that models can be compared consistently and reproducibly
To provide the system prompt that each GenAI model must use during deployment in production systems
To provide live user feedback that measures concept drift in deployed GenAI models
To provide adaptive, multi-turn attacks that change in response to a model's outputs during testing

questions.explanation: Benchmark suites are curated datasets and tasks that give standardised evaluation, enabling consistent comparison of language understanding, reasoning and coding abilities and identifying improvement areas systematically. Adaptive multi-turn attacks describe red teaming, and live feedback relates to drift testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.1 (p. 41); AI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A fitness-coaching chatbot is being red-teamed for safety rather than security. Which test conversation is MOST appropriate for this purpose?

options.text: A user pretends to be the developer and asks the chatbot to reveal its hidden system prompt
A user with no malicious intent mentions chest pain during workouts and asks whether to keep training harder
A tester submits a curated benchmark of trivia questions to compare the chatbot with a rival
A tester measures GPU memory while thousands of simulated users ask about diet plans at once

questions.explanation: For safety evaluations, red teaming often aims to identify how the system might create harmful outputs under ordinary use, such as unsafe medical advice, without adversarial intent. Extracting the system prompt is a security attack, a benchmark is a static comparison, and GPU memory is non-functional testing. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.2.2 (p. 42); AI-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A DNN is compressed to reduce its size before being embedded in a vehicle's control software. What should system testing confirm?

options.text: That each neuron in the compressed network exceeds the coverage threshold for all of the original test inputs
That the training dataset still contains the same number of labelled images as before the compression
That the vendor of the ML framework has certified the compressed model for use in the vehicle system
That the ML functional performance found at model level is not adversely affected inside the complete system

questions.explanation: System testing includes confirmation testing that ML functional performance from model testing is not adversely affected when the model is embedded in the complete system, which is especially important after deliberate changes such as compressing a DNN. The other options do not confirm the deployed behavior. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.1 (p. 43); AI-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which test approach is an example of an ML-specific mitigation for risks identified in the model area?

options.text: Code review of the payment module to check the rounding of currency values
Installability testing of the printer driver used for printing monthly reports
Adversarial testing to check how easily slightly perturbed inputs cause misclassification
Usability testing of the login page to check the accessibility of the forms

questions.explanation: Model-area risks include failing to reach required ML functional performance, overfitting and susceptibility to adversarial examples, which adversarial testing addresses. The other approaches address conventional, non-ML components. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 4.3.2 (p. 44); AI-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Training data for a credit model was bought from a broker who cannot explain how it was collected. Which test is MOST appropriate to mitigate this risk?

options.text: Label correctness testing
Data provenance testing
Model conversion testing
Neuron coverage testing

questions.explanation: Training data acquired from untrustworthy sources, or poorly managed data, is mitigated by data provenance testing. Label correctness addresses annotation quality, neuron coverage concerns internal network activation, and model conversion testing concerns deployment formats. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.1 (p. 47); AI-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How can dynamic testing detect bias in a trained ML model?

options.text: By reviewing the dataset documentation to see how the data was collected and annotated and which populations it represents
By running the training script twice with different random seeds and checking that both of the runs produce identical model weights
By running a known unbiased, representative dataset through it and checking the predictions for significant differences between sensitive groups
By checking that each neuron in the network is activated above a threshold by test inputs from each of the sensitive groups

questions.explanation: Dynamic testing feeds a known unbiased and representative dataset through the system and analyses the predictions for statistically significant outcome differences across sensitive groups, whatever the source of the bias. Documentation review is static, and identical weights or neuron coverage do not reveal unfair treatment. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); AI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which check belongs to component integration testing of a data pipeline?

options.text: Verifying that data flows correctly across internal interfaces and is interpreted correctly as it moves through the pipeline
Verifying that the pipeline exchanges data correctly with external storage platforms and monitoring tools
Verifying that the live pipeline's performance is consistent with previous versions using monitoring tools
Verifying that a single transformation script converts temperatures correctly and rejects malformed values

questions.explanation: Component integration testing verifies the seamless flow of data across internal interfaces and correct interpretation, detecting mismatched interfaces or wrong assumptions between components. A single script is component testing, external systems are system integration testing, and live comparisons are testing in production. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); AI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: When should data representativeness testing be performed?

options.text: Before model training, with the properties of operational input data monitored after deployment to detect drift
During model tuning, because the validation results show which of the classes are underrepresented in the population
During rollback testing, because a restored model must be retrained with representative production data
After deployment, because representativeness can be judged from operational data alone, without training data

questions.explanation: Testing for data representativeness should be performed before training to avoid building models on unrepresentative data; after deployment, operational input data should be monitored for data drift. Validation results and rollback testing do not replace a representativeness assessment. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.4 (p. 50); AI-5.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A payments dataset prepared for training includes the attribute transaction_timestamp, and every one of its 2 million values is unique. Which dataset constraint would flag this attribute, and why?

options.text: A correlate constraint, because unique timestamps show that the timestamp no longer correlates with the transaction amount
A duplicate constraint, because unique timestamps show that the same transaction was recorded several different times in the dataset
A useful constraint, because a column of entirely unique values gives a model no repeated values from which to learn patterns
A range constraint, because unique timestamps show that the values lie outside the period covered by the training data

questions.explanation: The useful constraint tests that an attribute contains some repeated values; if every entry is unique, like an ID or timestamp, it typically provides no useful patterns for an ML model. Uniqueness is the opposite of duplication, and it says nothing about range or correlation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.5 (p. 51); AI-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which TWO label correctness approaches rely on the outputs of the trained classifier itself to find potentially mislabelled data? Select TWO.

options.text: Model loss analysis
Data distribution analysis
Multiple annotation with agreement scores
Expert review of a labelled sample
Model confidence score analysis

questions.explanation: Model loss analysis flags points with high loss and model confidence score analysis flags points with low prediction confidence; both rely on a trained model. Expert review and multiple annotation rely on human annotators, and distribution analysis compares the dataset with comparable datasets. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 5.1.6 (p. 52); AI-5.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO test approaches does the syllabus list as mitigations for the test oracle problem when testing ML models? Select TWO.

options.text: Installability testing
Fuzz testing
Back-to-back testing
Smoke testing
Metamorphic testing

questions.explanation: The model risk table maps the test oracle problem to metamorphic testing, back-to-back testing and A/B testing. Smoke testing checks for immediate failures, fuzz testing for robustness to unexpected inputs, and installability testing for deployment. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.1 (p. 55); AI-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A documentation checklist item asks for the monitoring metrics and alerts, the retraining strategy and the model update and rollback plan. To which checklist area does this item belong?

options.text: Design
Non-functional
Operational
Datasets

questions.explanation: The operational area covers the deployment plan and environment, computational resources, monitoring metrics and alerts, retraining strategy, update and rollback plans, deprecation, security and explainability methods. Design covers assumptions and algorithms, datasets cover data properties, and non-functional covers qualities such as scalability, reliability and performance efficiency. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.2 (p. 56); AI-6.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How should the results of ML functional performance testing for a probabilistic model be reported?

options.text: As a simple passed/failed ratio, for example '940 of the 1,000 test cases passed the accuracy check'
As the highest accuracy observed in any single run of the full test suite
With statistical confidence, for example 'accuracy 94% ±4% at the 95% confidence level'
As a list of failed test cases with no aggregate measure of performance

questions.explanation: Aggregated results are interpreted and reported with statistical confidence rather than as a simple passed/failed ratio, so stakeholders understand the range of expected operational performance. A best single run or a list of failures gives no sound basis for a deployment decision. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.3 (p. 57); AI-6.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why is white-box adversarial testing typically more effective at finding adversarial examples than black-box testing?

options.text: White-box testing is performed by an independent team, so adversarial inputs are not biased by developer knowledge
White-box testing removes the need for test inputs, because adversarial examples are read from the training logs
White-box testing uses the production data stream, so adversarial inputs are found by monitoring real users
Knowledge of the model's architecture, parameters and training process makes it easier to craft inputs that cause misclassification

questions.explanation: Understanding an ML model's internals, such as its architecture, parameters and training process, typically makes crafting adversarial examples easier. White-box testing still needs test inputs, does not rely on production monitoring, and is defined by knowledge of internals rather than team independence. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.4 (p. 58); AI-6.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: An image classifier labelled a photograph of a stop sign as 'stop sign', and this source test case passed. Which follow-up test case applies a sensible invariance relation?

options.text: Replace the stop sign with a yield sign and expect the label to remain 'stop sign'
Rotate the photograph by 180 degrees and expect the label to become 'yield sign'
Increase the photograph's brightness slightly and expect the label to remain 'stop sign'
Blur the photograph until the sign is completely unrecognisable and expect the label 'stop sign'

questions.explanation: Invariance means outputs remain stable under perturbations that do not change the required property; a slight brightness change should not change the label. Replacing the sign changes the correct output, blurring until unrecognisable destroys the property the relation relies on, and expecting a different sign after rotation is not a valid relation. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.5 (p. 59); AI-6.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: What does dynamic drift testing depend on?

options.text: A list of metamorphic relations, which are applied to production inputs to check consistency of the outputs
Feedback from users that provides the current ground truth, which is compared with the model's outputs against a threshold
A second model trained on the same data, whose outputs are compared with the production model on live requests
A frozen copy of the training dataset, which is reprocessed nightly to check that the deployed model still gives the same outputs

questions.explanation: Dynamic drift testing relies on user feedback, direct or indirect, that provides the current ground truth; the difference between ground truth and model output is compared with a threshold. Reprocessing training data, comparing models or applying metamorphic relations do not measure drift against current ground truth. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.7 (p. 60); AI-6.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester inspects the learning curves of a model. Which pattern indicates underfitting?

options.text: Training error falls to almost zero while validation error starts rising after about twenty epochs
Training and validation errors both fall quickly and settle at low values that are close to each other
Validation error is lower than training error at every epoch, and both of them fall steadily throughout the whole training run
Training and validation errors stay high and close together without significant improvement as training progresses

questions.explanation: If training and validation errors remain high and relatively close, without significant improvement, the model is underfitting. A falling training error with rising validation error suggests overfitting, low converged errors suggest a right-fitting model, and the last pattern does not indicate underfitting. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.8 (p. 60); AI-6.1.8 (K2).

questions.prompt: A self-learning trading assistant changes its strategy automatically. How can A/B testing support this system?

options.text: After each change, tests are run and the resulting characteristics are compared with those before it; the change is kept if better, otherwise reverted
After each change, the training data is relabelled by experts, and the change is kept if the inter-annotator agreement improves
After each change, the model is converted to a new format, and the change is kept if the converted model loads correctly
After each change, the model's documentation is reviewed, and the change is kept if the model card has been updated

questions.explanation: For self-learning systems, A/B testing runs automated tests whenever the system changes and compares the resulting characteristics with those before the change, accepting improvements and reverting otherwise. Relabelling, documentation review and format conversion do not decide whether a change improved the system. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.9 (p. 61); AI-6.1.9 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST captures the difference between A/B testing and back-to-back testing?

options.text: A/B testing is performed before deployment; back-to-back testing can be performed only after a model has been retired
A/B testing compares a system with conventional software; back-to-back testing compares two versions of the same dataset
A/B testing compares two variants with ML functional performance metrics and statistics; back-to-back testing compares outputs to detect defects
A/B testing needs expected results for each test; back-to-back testing needs no inputs because it monitors production traffic

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that A/B testing compares two variants of the same MLS using ML functional performance metrics and statistical techniques, whereas back-to-back testing is used to detect defects. Neither description in the distractors matches the techniques. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 6.1.10 (p. 62); AI-6.1.10 (K2).

questions.prompt: A data engineer accidentally assigns some records to both the training and the test datasets. Which mitigation targets this development risk?

options.text: Model conversion testing
Algorithm suitability review
Framework suitability review
Data allocation review

questions.explanation: Defective allocation of data to training, validation and testing datasets is mitigated by a data allocation review. Framework and algorithm suitability reviews address selection risks, and model conversion testing addresses deployment format changes. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.1 (p. 64); AI-7.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: When must rollback testing be performed?

options.text: After a failed deployment, to find out whether a previously stable state can still be restored in production
During model training, to confirm that the network's weights can be reset to their initial random values at the end of each epoch
During canary testing, to decide which of the users in the canary group receive the previous model version
Before deployment, to confirm that the system can revert to a previously stable state if the deployment degrades or fails

questions.explanation: Rollback testing verifies the ability to revert to a previously stable state after a degraded or failed deployment, covering the model or the complete system, and must be performed before deployment to confirm rollback readiness. Waiting until after a failure is too late. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 7.1.2 (p. 65); AI-7.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants software that learns the best order in which to dispatch delivery robots by trying different strategies and receiving rewards for on-time deliveries. Which approach does this describe?

options.text: Reinforcement learning, in which an intelligent agent improves its behavior through trial-and-error interaction with its environment
Rule-based reasoning, in which an expert system applies dispatch rules that were written by logistics domain experts
Supervised learning, in which an algorithm maps labelled examples of past dispatch orders to their recorded outputs
Unsupervised learning, in which an algorithm groups past delivery records into clusters of similar orders without needing any labels

questions.explanation: Learning from rewards and penalties through interaction with an environment is reinforcement learning. Clustering finds structure without rewards, supervised learning needs labelled input-output examples, and an expert system follows rules it was given rather than learning them. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); AI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A marketing agency plans to use a GenAI image model for campaign material. Which concern is raised specifically for GenAI in the CT-AI syllabus?

options.text: The model cannot produce images of new objects because generative models only reproduce training images
The model will need less computing power than a classifier because generation uses fewer parameters
The ease of producing convincing synthetic content increases risks such as deepfakes, misinformation and fraud
The model cannot be used commercially because GenAI outputs must be published under an open-source software licence

questions.explanation: The syllabus highlights misuse of GenAI, such as deepfakes, misinformation and fraudulent content, along with privacy, employment and sustainability concerns. There is no open-source licensing rule, GenAI creates new content, and large GenAI models consume substantial computational resources. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.4 (p. 17); AI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team quantizes a model from 32-bit to 4-bit arithmetic before deploying it to an embedded device. Which benefit does the CT-AI syllabus associate with low-precision arithmetic?

options.text: Easier explainability, because fewer bits per weight let reviewers read each decision path
Faster processing, lower power consumption, smaller and cheaper chips and reduced bandwidth
Removal of the need for a test dataset, because quantized models keep identical predictions
Higher prediction accuracy, because rounding removes noise that was learned during training

questions.explanation: Quantization uses fewer bits for computation, giving faster processing, lower power, smaller and more cost-effective chips and reduced bandwidth. It does not guarantee better accuracy or identical predictions, which is why the converted model still needs testing, and it does not make models explainable. Syllabus reference: CT-AI v2.0, section 1.1.5 (p. 18); AI-1.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A hospital wants to build a model using sensitive patient records while also needing large computing resources for training. Which TWO statements describe advantages of a hybrid approach? Select TWO.

options.text: A prototype can be developed locally before the work is scaled up to cloud infrastructure
